description: Session syllabus seed for CourseLevelSessions. Match each level on topicName + level to fill in courseLevelId before importing.
source: Shared course Drive folder, level outline documents
parentCopyStatus: Parent copy authored for every session that has source material. Levels absent from this file (Cybersecurity, EV3, Python 3 and 4, Flutter) have no per-session outline to work from.

sessions.title: Introduction to Mobile Apps
keyConcepts: Steps to create an app (design → code)
Introduction to coding and block coding
activities: Create "Hello It's Me" app with
Button
Label
Text-to-speech
Angry Birds programming game
sessions.task: Build a personal intro app (name, age, school, hobby)
sessions.parentSummary: Your child met MIT App Inventor, the tool we use to build phone apps all term. Instead of typing code they drag blocks together, so the logic is real but the typing isn't in the way. They built their first working app: a button that speaks a short introduction out loud.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to run their intro app on your phone and talk you through what each block does.
sessions.content: What building an app involves, and the two halves of App Inventor: the Designer, where components are placed on a screen, and the Blocks editor, where their behaviour is written. Every component has properties — a label's text, its colour, its size — which can be set in the Designer or changed from blocks while the app runs.

sessions.title: Two-Button Game
keyConcepts: Horizontal, vertical, and table arrangement layouts
activities: Build a two-button game app
Debugging practice
sessions.task: Add up/down buttons to the project
sessions.parentSummary: This week was about what happens when someone taps the screen, and how to arrange things on it so an app doesn't look accidental. Your child built a small two-button game, then spent time debugging it — working out why something doesn't behave is half of programming.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask what went wrong the first time and how they tracked it down.
sessions.content: The maths and comparison blocks: equal, not equal, greater than, less than, and the two that include equality. Each returns true or false, which is what lets the app decide. The two-button game is built on nothing more than that.

sessions.title: Age Calculator
activities: Create age calculator app
"Collect Treasure" game
sessions.task: Add text-to-speech for age output
sessions.parentSummary: Your child built an app that asks for a birthday and works out an age from it, using a real date picker — the same control you see in booking apps.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Give them your birthday and let the app tell you how old you are.
sessions.content: The DatePicker, a button that opens a calendar so the user can choose a date, with the Clock component doing the arithmetic on it. Buttons, labels, date pickers and layouts together make an age calculator.

sessions.title: Piano App
activities: Build a piano app with
Buttons
Images
Player for notes
sessions.task: Modify piano notes and design
sessions.parentSummary: An app that makes sound. Your child built a piano from image buttons, and learned the difference between information the whole app can see and information only one part of it can — a distinction that prevents a lot of bugs later.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to play you something on their piano app.
sessions.content: Variables, and the difference between the two kinds. A global variable can be read and changed anywhere in the app; a local one exists only inside the block that declared it. The piano app uses them to keep track of what is playing.

sessions.title: Simple Calculator
activities: Create calculator app
Flappy Bird game exercise
sessions.task: Add power (^) calculation button
sessions.parentSummary: Taking numbers a user types in and doing something with them. Your child built a working calculator, then extended it with a power button for homework.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Test their calculator with an awkward sum and see whether it holds up.
sessions.content: The logic blocks and what equality really means: two numbers match if their values match, so 1 equals 1.0, but two pieces of text must match character for character, so banana is not Banana. The calculator project depends on getting that right.

sessions.title: Quiz App
activities: Build quiz app
Loops with Rey and BB-8 game
sessions.task: Add high-score variable
sessions.parentSummary: Two larger ideas this week: lists, which hold many items under one name, and procedures — naming a chunk of work so it can be reused instead of rebuilt. Your child built a quiz app that runs through questions and keeps score.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to add a question you'd know the answer to, then play it.
sessions.content: Algorithms, introduced through the order of steps in making a sandwich, then applied to a quiz app: present a question, compare the answer, update the score, move on. Getting the order wrong is the bug.

sessions.title: Snake Game
activities: Develop Snake game
"Swimming Fish" coding challenge
sessions.task: Add Level 2 screen (unlocks at 10 points)
sessions.parentSummary: Game building starts here. Your child learned that a phone screen is really a grid of coordinates, and moved a character around it. The result was a working Snake game.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to explain why the snake moves. It is arithmetic, not magic, and they can show you.
sessions.content: The Canvas as a coordinate grid, and the ImageSprite: a graphic placed on it that can be touched and dragged, collide with other sprites and with the edges, and move on its own. The snake game is built from a canvas, sprites, a ball and a score label.

sessions.title: Bouncing Ball Game
activities: Bouncing ball game
Nested loops with Bee game
sessions.task: Add multiple balls and improve design
sessions.parentSummary: A bouncing ball game spread across more than one screen. Apps that move between pages have to hand information from one to the next, which is harder than it sounds.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to show you both screens and explain how the app decides to switch.
sessions.content: The Ball, a round sprite with the same collision and movement behaviour as an image sprite. The bouncing ball game is about what happens at the edges of the canvas and what happens when two sprites meet.

sessions.title: Shopping List
activities: Create shopping list app
Variables with Bee exercise
sessions.task: Enhance app design + internet safety tips
sessions.parentSummary: The first app that remembers anything after it closes. Your child built a shopping list that saves itself to the phone. We also spent part of the session on internet safety.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask what they learned about staying safe online — it was part of the lesson, not an extra.
sessions.content: The ListView, which displays a list of text or images on screen, and TinyDB, which stores data on the device so it survives the app closing. Together they make a shopping list that is still there tomorrow.

sessions.title: Drawing App
activities: Build drawing application
Minecraft conditionals game
sessions.task: Research machine learning + add more colors to the project
sessions.parentSummary: A drawing app your child designed themselves, which meant thinking about what makes an app pleasant to use rather than merely functional.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Draw something on their app, then ask them what they would change about the design.
sessions.content: The Canvas used for drawing rather than for games: a touch-sensitive panel whose background, paint colour and size can all be set, with the user's finger as the brush. The session also makes the point that an app is made for someone to use, so knowing who that is comes first.

sessions.title: Recipe App
activities: Develop recipe app with voice input
"If" conditions with Bee game
sessions.task: Add more recipes to the project
sessions.parentSummary: Your child built an app you talk to. It listens, turns speech into text and finds a matching recipe. We also introduced machine learning at a basic level.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask it for a recipe out loud and see how well it copes with your voice.
sessions.content: The Spinner, a dropdown that presents a set of choices, and the speech recogniser, which turns what the user says into text the app can act on. The recipe app uses both.

sessions.title: Texting App
activities: Build texting application
Minecraft debugging challenge
sessions.task: Improve app design + final quiz
sessions.steamTopic: How the internet stores and sends data
sessions.parentSummary: The last app of the level: one that picks a contact and sends a message. The session finished with a quiz covering the whole term. Your child can now build a working Android app starting from a blank screen.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask which of the twelve apps they are proudest of, and why.
sessions.content: The Texting component, which sends a message to a number and raises an event when one arrives. Combined with the contact picker and a list view, it makes a working texting app — and the level closes on how data actually travels.

sessions.title: Advanced Calculator
activities: Build an advanced calculator using labels, buttons, arrangements and a Notifier
Add percentage, sign toggle and clear, and handle division by zero
sessions.task: Add % (percentage), +/- (sign toggle), and C (clear) functions
sessions.parentSummary: Level 2 opens by rebuilding something familiar properly. Your child extended a calculator with a backspace key and, more importantly, made it cope with being asked to divide by zero. Handling the moment a user does something unexpected is what separates a demo from an app.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Try to break their calculator. If it refuses politely instead of crashing, that was the lesson.
sessions.content: Procedures, which collect a sequence of blocks into a named group that can be called repeatedly instead of rebuilt. Alongside them the Notifier component, used to show a message or warning, and the control blocks that handle if and else.

sessions.title: Voice Translator
activities: Build a voice translator between English and French
Change the screen colour to match the language being spoken
sessions.task: Add screen color changes on translation
sessions.parentSummary: A translator app. Your child combined speech recognition with text-to-speech so the app listens in one language and answers in another.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Say a sentence in English and let it come back in French.
sessions.content: The Translator component, which sends text to a server at MIT and returns it in another language, so the app needs an internet connection to work. Combined with speech recognition and text-to-speech, the app can listen in one language and answer aloud in another.

sessions.title: Voice Assistant
activities: Build a voice assistant that answers set questions and searches the web
Add a button that repeats the assistant's last message
sessions.task: Add message repeat function
sessions.parentSummary: A voice assistant that remembers your name, answers set questions and can search the web for anything it doesn't know.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask it something it wasn't programmed for and see how it responds.
sessions.content: Building an assistant that reacts to what it hears. The app compares the recognised speech against known phrases and answers accordingly, falling back to a web search through the WebViewer when it does not recognise the request.

sessions.title: Ball Bar Game
activities: Build a brick-breaking Ball Bar game with a Canvas, sprites and paddle controls
Add a sound effect when the ball hits something
sessions.task: Add collision sound effects
sessions.parentSummary: A brick-breaking game with paddle controls, win and lose conditions, and a speed that climbs as you progress. Deciding when a player has won is a surprisingly fiddly piece of logic.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Play a round and ask them how the app knows the game is over.
sessions.content: The ImageSprite: a graphic placed on a Canvas that can react to touches and drags, collide with other sprites and with the edges of the Canvas, and move on its own. This is the foundation of every game in the level.

sessions.title: IQ Test App
activities: Build an IQ test app with voice answers and score tracking
Greet the user by name when the quiz starts
sessions.task: Personalize start message ("Hello [Name]...")
sessions.parentSummary: An IQ quiz that accepts answers spoken aloud and keeps score across questions. Your child worked with lists and question indexing to move through the quiz in order.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Take their quiz and let them tell you your score.
sessions.content: Arrangements, which control where components sit on screen. A Horizontal Arrangement groups components side by side like a row; nesting arrangements is how a designed layout is built rather than a stack of controls.

sessions.title: Chase Food Game
activities: Build a Chase Food game with a Canvas, sprites, labels and a Notifier
Program the food to move by itself
Draw a flowchart of the game logic
sessions.task: Design game flowchart
sessions.parentSummary: A chase game where the food moves by itself, which meant writing rules for something that isn't controlled by the player. Your child also drew a flowchart of the game logic before building it.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask to see the flowchart. Planning before building is the habit we are trying to form.
sessions.content: Putting layout together with sprite movement to build a game where something moves on its own rather than only responding to the player. The session also introduces flowcharts for planning the game logic before building it.

sessions.title: Chatting App
activities: Build a chat app with a Button, Label, ListPicker, TextBox, ListView and CloudDB
Make messages disappear after a few seconds using a Clock
sessions.task: Add timed message disappearance
sessions.steamTopic: How a keyboard, a mouse and a touchscreen work
sessions.parentSummary: A chat app, and the first time your child stored data in the cloud rather than on the phone. That is the difference between a note to yourself and a message someone else can receive.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to explain where their messages actually go when they press send.
sessions.content: The ListView, which displays a list of text or images on screen, and the difference between storing data on the device and storing it in the cloud — the difference between a note to yourself and a message someone else receives.

sessions.title: Book Reading App
activities: Build a book reading app with a Label, Button, TextBox and WebViewer
Add a TextBox so users can save a favourite book
sessions.task: Add favorite books database
sessions.parentSummary: A book reader that keeps your place, reads aloud, and pulls content from the web. Bookmarking meant saving information and finding it again later.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to read you a page using the app's own voice.
sessions.content: Databases. A database stores information that survives the app closing, unlike a variable, which is forgotten the moment the app stops. Combined with the WebViewer to pull book content from the internet.

sessions.title: Voice Note App
activities: Build a voice note app with speech recognition, text-to-speech and File storage
Add playback with adjustable speed
sessions.task: Add adjustable playback speed
sessions.parentSummary: A voice note app that records, saves to a file and plays back. Working with files on a phone is a different skill from working with a database.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Record a message for them on it and have them play it back.
sessions.content: The File component, a non-visible component for reading and writing files on the device. Working with files is a different skill from working with a database: the app manages the storage itself.

sessions.title: Fruit Ninja Game
activities: Build a Fruit Ninja game with a Canvas, buttons, sprites and arrangements
Add a power-up that makes all fruits explode
sessions.task: Add explosive fruit power-up
sessions.parentSummary: A fruit-slicing game with sprites that spawn on their own, touch detection and a combo system. This one has a lot of moving parts running at once.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Play it and ask them what happens behind the scenes when your finger crosses a fruit.
sessions.content: More advanced sprite work: spawning objects during play, detecting touches across a Canvas, and tracking a score that changes as the game runs.

sessions.title: Multiplayer Racing
activities: Build a multiplayer racing game with Sound, Player, Firebase and a Notifier
Add a speed boost or shield power-up
sessions.task: Implement speed boost/shield
sessions.parentSummary: A racing game two people can play at the same time on different phones, kept in step through the cloud. Multiplayer is a genuine step up in difficulty.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Race them. Ask how both phones stay in agreement about who is winning.
sessions.content: Sound, added either as short clips for events like a collision or as longer files for background music. Combined with Firebase so two players on different devices stay in step.

sessions.title: Data Storage App
activities: Build a data storage app with a table arrangement, TextBox, Button and Firebase
Compare how humans learn with how machines learn
sessions.task: Compare human vs machine learning
sessions.parentSummary: The level closes with a data storage app that can create, read, update and delete records — the four operations behind nearly every app that saves anything. We also compared how people learn with how machines do.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them what they think a computer is genuinely better at than a person, and what it is worse at.
sessions.content: FirebaseDB, which stores and retrieves values under tags through a web service, so data written on one device can be read on another. The four operations behind almost every app that saves anything: create, read, update and delete.

sessions.title: Flashlight & Tic Tac Toe
activities: Build flashlight app with ON/OFF toggle
Develop Tic Tac Toe game with table arrangement
sessions.task: Add click sound effects to flashlight
sessions.parentSummary: Level 3 is about apps that use the phone itself. Your child built a flashlight that controls the real torch, which meant asking the phone for permission first, and a Tic Tac Toe game alongside it.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask why an app has to ask permission before using the camera or torch.
sessions.content: Extensions: components that other people have written and published as .aix files, imported into a project to do things App Inventor cannot do on its own — Bluetooth, Firebase, machine learning. The flashlight and noughts and crosses apps put the idea to work.

sessions.title: Battery Monitor
activities: Create battery info app displaying
Charge level
Temperature
Voltage
sessions.task: Add low-battery (20%) notifier
sessions.parentSummary: An app that reads the phone's own battery — level, temperature and voltage — and warns when it runs low. Your child is now reading data out of the device rather than only putting things on the screen.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask what temperature their phone battery is running at right now.
sessions.content: Reading the state of the device itself rather than the user's input. The battery monitor reports the charge level and reacts to it, which means the app is responding to something it did not cause.

sessions.title: Camera & Gallery App
activities: Build hybrid camera app with
Photo capture
Gallery integration
TinyDB storage
sessions.task: Combine ImagePicker with Camera
sessions.parentSummary: A camera app that takes photos, pulls existing ones from the gallery and stores them. Handling image files is noticeably harder than handling text.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Take a photo with their app and ask where it gets saved.
sessions.content: The Camera component, and storing what it captures. TinyDB keeps the images on the device so they are still there next time, and the ImagePicker lets the user choose one they already had.

sessions.title: Account Management
activities: Develop sign-up/login system with
Google OAuth
Secure password storage
sessions.task: Implement 8-character password validation
sessions.parentSummary: Sign-up and login, including Google accounts and password rules. Your child learned why passwords are never stored as plain text, which is a genuinely important idea.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them why an app should not be able to tell you your own password.
sessions.content: Account management: a sign-up screen, a sign-in screen, and the stored credentials that connect them. Validating a password before accepting it is the point — an app that accepts anything is not really checking.

sessions.title: Escape Chicken Game
activities: Create side-scroller game with
Obstacle avoidance
Score tracking
Multi-screen flow
sessions.task: Add customizable player costumes
sessions.parentSummary: A side-scrolling game with obstacles, scoring and several screens, built on a timer that drives the animation.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Play it and ask them to beat your score.
sessions.content: Apps with more than one screen, and how to move between them with the 'open another screen' block. The escape chicken game uses a canvas, sprites, a clock for timing, a player for sound and TinyDB for the score.

sessions.title: NASA API Explorer
activities: Build app fetching NASA API data
Display space images/info
sessions.task: Expand API data utilization
sessions.parentSummary: Your child's app now talks to NASA. It sends a request over the internet, receives data back and displays the images and information it finds. This is how most real apps get their content.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to show you today's space image and explain where it came from.
sessions.content: APIs. An API is how one program asks another for information; the Web component sends the request, and an event fires when the response arrives so the app can read it. The NASA app pulls real data over the internet.

sessions.title: Weather App
activities: Develop weather app with
City search
Voice input option
sessions.task: Add speech-to-text city input
sessions.parentSummary: A weather app you can search by city, or ask out loud. It combines live internet data with voice input, pulling together two things learned separately.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask it for the weather somewhere far away and see if it agrees with your phone.
sessions.content: A second API project, this time weather. The user types a city, the app requests the forecast and displays what comes back — the same pattern as the NASA app, which is the point of doing it twice.

sessions.title: AI Drawing Bot
activities: Create art generator with
Prompt input
Image display
sessions.task: Implement regenerate function
sessions.parentSummary: An app that generates artwork from a written description using an AI image service. Your child learned how the wording of a request changes what comes back.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Give it a description and see what it produces. Try changing one word.
sessions.content: The ImageBot, a non-visible component that sends a description to DALL-E 2 and gets a generated image back. The app takes text from the user, requests the picture and displays it, with text-to-speech alongside.

sessions.title: GPS Tracker
activities: Build tracker with
Live location
Map markers
sessions.task: Save coordinates to Firebase
sessions.parentSummary: A location tracker using the phone's GPS, showing position on a map and saving coordinates to the cloud.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them how accurate it is, and what the two numbers on screen actually mean.
sessions.content: Location. The location sensor reports latitude, longitude, altitude and speed from GPS or the network, and the Map component displays an interactive map with markers on it. Together they make a tracker that can share where you are.

sessions.title: Object Detection
activities: Create vision app with
Custom image training
Themed UI
sessions.task: Enhance classifier UI design
sessions.parentSummary: An app that recognises objects through the camera, trained on images your child supplied. They saw directly that a model is only as good as what it was shown.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Show it something it wasn't trained on and watch it guess wrongly. That is the lesson.
sessions.content: Machine learning inside the app. The Personal Image Classifier is trained on labelled photographs and then recognises what the camera is pointed at, with the result driving what the app does next. A splash screen is added while the model loads.

sessions.title: Mental Health App
activities: Build wellness app with
Mood logging
AI responses
sessions.task: Add introductory splash screen
sessions.parentSummary: A wellbeing app with mood tracking and a chatbot that responds. Thinking about how an app should speak to someone having a difficult day is a design skill as much as a technical one.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them how they decided what the app should say back.
sessions.content: The Chatbot component, which holds a conversation with the user — reading what they type, working out what it means and answering. Built into a mental health app, where the answer matters more than the mechanism.

sessions.title: Currency Converter
activities: Develop converter with
Real-time rates
Multi-currency support
sessions.task: Improve app visual design
sessions.parentSummary: The final app of the course: a currency converter using live exchange rates. Your child has now built apps that use the camera, GPS, voice, cloud storage, AI and live internet data.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to convert something into another currency, then ask what they want to build next.
sessions.content: The final project brings the API work back: a currency converter that requests live exchange rates from a web service, reads the JSON that comes back and calculates with it.

sessions.title: Foundations of Electronics
activities: Identify LED polarity (long/short leads)
Calculate resistor values using Ohm’s Law
Build a basic LED circuit with a 9V battery
sessions.task: Research and present the history of electricity
sessions.parentSummary: Before any code, electricity. Your child learned what voltage, current and resistance actually are, how to read the coloured bands on a resistor, and built a simple LED circuit powered by a battery.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them why an LED needs a resistor next to it. Without one it burns out, and they can tell you why.
sessions.content: Electricity from the ground up, taught through the water analogy: a tank of water is the charge, the pressure at the end of the hose is the voltage, and the flow through it is the current. Resistance is what narrows the hose. Ohm's law ties the three together, and the session ends on resistors in series and in parallel — plus why static from your hands can destroy a component.

sessions.title: Introduction to Arduino Boards
keyConcepts: Arduino Uno components (digital/analog pins, power LED, USB port)
activities: Explore Arduino Uno board layout
Create binary bracelets using ASCII values
Simulate a simple LED blink project
sessions.task: Present real-world uses of Arduino
sessions.steamTopic: Microprocessors and the chips inside a computer
sessions.parentSummary: The Arduino board itself — what each pin does, how a breadboard connects things, and how computers represent letters as numbers. Your child made a binary bracelet spelling something in code.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to write your name in binary. They have the method.
sessions.content: What an Arduino actually is. A microcontroller is a whole tiny computer on one chip — powerful enough to run motors, read sensors and drive a display — as opposed to a microprocessor, which is only the processing part. The Arduino Uno is a circuit built around one of those chips, with digital pins that read on-or-off signals and analog pins that read a voltage level.

sessions.title: Digital Output
activities: Program a single LED to blink
Alternate blinking between two LEDs
Simulate a traffic light sequence
sessions.task: Explain how programming is used in everyday devices
sessions.parentSummary: The first programs. Your child made an LED blink, then two LEDs alternate, then built a working traffic light sequence. Getting a physical object to obey code for the first time is a good moment.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to explain what the board is doing in the gap between blinks.
sessions.content: What programming is, and how a computer stores what it is given. Binary uses two states because a circuit has two: 0 is a low voltage, 1 is high. ASCII maps text onto those numbers. Variables are the labels put on stored information, with rules about naming them, and the main types are numbers, strings and booleans.

sessions.title: Analog Inputs & Outputs
activities: Control LED brightness using a potentiometer
Build a dark-activated LED circuit with a photoresistor
sessions.task: Present applications of potentiometers in real life
sessions.parentSummary: The difference between a switch, which is on or off, and a dial, which is anywhere in between. Your child controlled LED brightness with a knob and built a light that comes on when the room goes dark.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask where they have seen a light that switches itself on at dusk.
sessions.content: Analog signals, which carry a range of values rather than just on or off — sound levels, light levels, the position of a dial. The potentiometer is the example: turning it changes its resistance, the Arduino reads that as a number, and the number sets the brightness of an LED.

sessions.title: Buzzer and Sound
keyConcepts: Frequency and sound waves (measured in Hz)
activities: Connect a buzzer to Arduino in Tinkercad
Create a traffic light system with buzzer tones
Change tones based on LED states
sessions.task: Research and present buzzer applications (e.g., alarms, music)
sessions.parentSummary: Sound. Your child learned that pitch is just frequency, connected a buzzer, and added warning tones to the traffic light from an earlier week.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to make the buzzer play a high note and a low note, and explain what changed.
sessions.content: The buzzer — a component that produces a tone when a signal is applied — and how the pitch changes with the frequency sent to it. Built into the traffic light project from the previous sessions, so the lights now make a sound as they change.

sessions.title: Push-Button Input
activities: Connect a push-button to control an LED
Use two buttons to control two LEDs
Simulate a doorbell with a buzzer
sessions.task: Explore real-world uses of push-buttons (e.g., elevators, keyboards)
sessions.parentSummary: Input from a person. Your child wired push-buttons to control LEDs and built a working doorbell. This is the first time their circuit reacts to someone rather than running on its own.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them how the board can tell the difference between a button pressed and one released.
sessions.content: The push-button, a mechanical switch that completes a circuit while it is held down and breaks it when released. Reading a button means reading a pin, deciding what the value means and acting on it — which is the first real algorithm in the level: take an input, apply a condition, produce an output.

sessions.title: Digital Input: Sensors
keyConcepts: Types of sensors (ultrasonic, temperature, PIR motion)
activities: Build a "Catch the Thief" circuit with motion sensor, LED, and buzzer
Measure distance with an ultrasonic sensor
Detect motion with a PIR sensor
sessions.task: presentation about previous sessions
sessions.parentSummary: Sensors — ultrasonic, motion and temperature. Your child built a Catch the Thief alarm that detects movement and responds with light and sound.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Walk past their alarm and let it catch you.
sessions.content: Sensors as a family, and the passive infrared sensor in detail: it measures the infrared energy given off by a warm body, and triggers when that reading changes sharply. The session also covers the practical side — the pin headers and the male and female jumper wires that connect everything.

sessions.title: Arduino IDE and C++ Basics
activities: Write a traffic light program with push-button and buzzer
Debug code using the serial monitor
Experiment with variable types
sessions.task: Research Arduino board variants (e.g., Nano, Mega)
sessions.parentSummary: Moving from drag-and-drop to writing real C++ code in the Arduino editor. Your child also met the serial monitor, which lets you see what a program is thinking while it runs — the main tool for finding bugs.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them how they find out why a program is misbehaving.
sessions.content: Leaving the drag-and-drop simulator for the Arduino IDE and real C++. Five functions do most of the work: pinMode sets a pin to input or output, digitalWrite and digitalRead handle on-or-off signals, and analogWrite and analogRead handle values across a range.

sessions.title: C++ Variables and Data Types
activities: Create a program to add two integers
Calculate decimal division using float
sessions.task: Build a program to calculate the cart cost
sessions.parentSummary: Variables and number types in C++, and why a program needs to be told whether something is a whole number or a decimal before it can do the sum.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask what happens if you divide 7 by 2 and the program is expecting a whole number.
sessions.content: Variables in C++, which need a declared type — int, float, char, boolean — before they can be used, and are case-sensitive. The arithmetic operators are covered alongside, including modulus, increment and decrement.

sessions.title: Conditionals and Operators
activities: Assign grades based on marks (A/B/C)
Check if the sum of two numbers equals 10
sessions.task: Design a program to determine the oldest among three ages
sessions.parentSummary: Decisions in code. Your child wrote programs that assign grades from marks and compare ages, using conditions chained together.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to describe how their grade program decides between a B and a C.
sessions.content: Making the program decide. Comparison operators produce true or false, if and else if choose between paths, and constants declared with const or #define give a fixed value a name so a pin number is written once rather than scattered through the code. The difference between a global and a local variable is covered here too.

sessions.title: Loops in C++
activities: Print numbers 0–100 with while
Create an array and access its fourth element
Use nested loops to print patterns
sessions.task: Draw a flowchart for a login system
sessions.parentSummary: Loops and arrays — repeating work, and storing a row of values under one name. Your child also drew a flowchart for a login system.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask to see the flowchart and follow it through with a wrong password.
sessions.content: For loops, nested loops, and break and continue for leaving a loop early or skipping one pass. Then servo motors, which hold a precise angle: the angle is set by the width of the pulse sent to the control pin, which is why they are used wherever position matters.

sessions.title: Functions and Servo Motors
activities: Write functions to rotate servo to 0° and 180°
Combine servo with push-button input
Simulate a robotic arm movement
sessions.task: Quiz on level 1
sessions.parentSummary: The level ends with functions and a servo motor, so the code now moves something physically. Your child simulated a robotic arm driven by a button, and sat a quiz on the whole level.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to show you the arm moving and explain what tells it where to stop.
sessions.content: While and do-while loops — the second always runs once before it checks — and functions: a named block of code that only runs when it is called, with parameters for passing information in. The level closes by combining the two.

sessions.title: Introduction to Sensors & Binary Numbers
keyConcepts: Binary numbers (bits, bytes) and their role in computing
activities: Convert binary numbers to decimal (e.g.,  → 170)
Simulate an LED binary counter in Tinkercad
sessions.task: Convert more binary numbers to decimal numbers
sessions.parentSummary: Level 2 begins with how computers count. Your child converted binary to decimal and built an LED counter that displays numbers in binary.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them what 1010 means. It is ten, and they can show you why.
sessions.content: Sensors compared to human senses, and the split that matters in practice: a digital sensor reports on or off, an analog sensor reports a value across a range. Binary numbers are covered properly here, since a sensor reading arrives as one, and the class builds an LED binary counter to see it.

sessions.title: Seven-Segment Displays
activities: Count up/down (0–9) using a seven-segment display
sessions.task: Display custom characters (e.g., "H" for "HELLO")
sessions.parentSummary: Seven-segment displays — the blocky numerals on microwaves and clocks. Your child made one count up and down, then spell out letters.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to make it show a letter and explain which segments switch on.
sessions.content: The seven-segment display: seven LEDs arranged so that lighting the right combination forms any digit from 0 to 9. Each segment needs its own resistor and pin, and the common leg goes to ground or to power depending on whether the part is common cathode or common anode.

sessions.title: Light Sensors (LDR & IR)
activities: Build a dark-activated LED using an LDR
Detect motion with an IR sensor and trigger an LED/buzzer
sessions.task: Research ultrasonic sensors and their use in robotics
sessions.steamTopic: Light and how it is detected
sessions.parentSummary: Light sensors. Your child built a lamp that reacts to darkness and a motion detector using infrared, the same technology as a television remote.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them how a TV remote and a burglar alarm use the same kind of light you cannot see.
sessions.content: Two light sensors. The LDR changes resistance with the light falling on it, so it connects to an analog pin and reports a range. The infrared sensor detects reflected infrared and reports whether something is in front of it, so it connects to a digital pin.

sessions.title: Proximity & Distance Sensors (Ultrasonic)
activities: Measure distance and display it on the serial monitor
Create a theremin-like buzzer with variable pitch based on distance
sessions.task: Compare DC vs. AC motors in industrial applications
sessions.parentSummary: Measuring distance with sound, the way a bat does. Your child calculated distance from how long an echo takes to return, then built an instrument whose pitch changes as your hand moves.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Move your hand towards their sensor and listen to the note change.
sessions.content: The ultrasonic sensor, which measures distance by emitting a pulse of sound too high to hear and timing how long the echo takes to return. Distance comes out of that timing, and the session uses it to control an LED and to change the tone of a buzzer as something gets closer.

sessions.title: DC Motors & H-Bridge (L293D)
activities: Control motor direction using push buttons
sessions.task: Build a two-wheeled robot chassis (simulated or physical)
sessions.parentSummary: Motors. Your child learned how to make a motor turn both ways using a driver circuit, and started building a two-wheeled robot chassis.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask why a motor needs a special chip between it and the board.
sessions.content: Driving motors. A DC motor needs more current than an Arduino pin can supply, so an L293D motor driver sits between them: the Arduino sends a small control signal and the driver switches the real power, which is also what makes reversing the direction possible. One driver runs two motors.

sessions.title: Soil Moisture Sensors
activities: Read Soil Moisture Sensor measurements in serial
Read Soil Moisture Sensor measurements in serial in percentage
Automate a plant watering system (simulated)
sessions.task: Create a soil moisture alert system with LEDs (Green/Yellow/Red)
sessions.parentSummary: A soil moisture sensor and an automatic plant watering system. Your child had to calibrate it, because dry soil does not read the same in every pot.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them what reading their sensor gives for a watered plant versus a dry one.
sessions.content: The soil moisture sensor, whose two-pronged probe acts as a resistor that changes with the water around it. It offers both a digital output — wet or dry against a threshold — and an analog one, giving an actual reading, which is what an irrigation system needs.

sessions.title: Temperature & Humidity Sensors (DHT11, DS18B20)
keyConcepts: DHT11 vs. DHT22 vs. DS18B20 (accuracy, range)
activities: Monitor room temperature/humidity and log data to serial
sessions.task: Research the difference between DHT11, DHT22 and DS18B20
sessions.parentSummary: Temperature and humidity sensors, and comparing several types on accuracy and range. Choosing the right component for a job is an engineering decision, not just a wiring one.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them which sensor they would pick for a greenhouse, and why.
sessions.content: Measuring temperature and humidity. A thermistor is a resistor whose value changes with temperature; the DS18B20 does the conversion itself and hands back a digital reading; the DHT11 and DHT22 report temperature and humidity together, differing in range and accuracy.

sessions.title: LCD Displays
activities: Display sensor data (e.g., temperature) on an LCD
Display name and age on LCD
sessions.task: Research I2C LCD advantages over standard LCDs
sessions.parentSummary: An LCD screen, so projects can report their own readings instead of needing a computer attached. Your child displayed live sensor data on it.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to put your name on the screen.
sessions.content: The LCD, a flat panel display that uses liquid crystals, wired through a set of data and control pins. Once the display works, the temperature and humidity readings from the previous session have somewhere to go other than the serial monitor.

sessions.title: Keypads & Input Systems
activities: Use the keypad with Serial monitor
Print keypad inputs to an LCD
sessions.task: Present different keypad types (membrane, mechanical)
sessions.parentSummary: A keypad for entering numbers and letters, and the problem of debouncing — a single press that the board reads as several, and how to stop it.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask why a computer might think you pressed a button three times when you pressed it once.
sessions.content: The keypad, a grid of buttons wired as rows and columns: pressing one connects a single row to a single column, and the Arduino works out which key it was from that pair. A 3x4 keypad needs seven pins, a 4x4 needs eight. Combined with the LCD, it makes a working calculator.

sessions.title: Advanced Sensors & Applications
sessions.task: Research about environmental sensors
sessions.parentSummary: The level closes with advanced sensors: gas and air quality, fingerprint and card readers, and GPS. Your child now has a working sense of what can be measured and how.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them what they would like to measure at home, and what sensor it would take.
sessions.content: The level closes on the sensors behind everyday technology: biometric sensors, which capture a face, fingerprint or iris as data a computer can match, and the sound sensor, which works like an ear — a microphone, a peak detector and an amplifier.

sessions.title: Communication & Protocols (UART)
activities: Send messages between two Arduinos using UART
sessions.task: Trigger an LED on Arduino 2 based on distance data from Arduino 1 (ultrasonic sensor)
sessions.steamTopic: How Amazon uses robots in its warehouses
sessions.parentSummary: Level 3 is about making devices talk to each other. Your child sent messages between two Arduino boards over a wire, then had one board switch on a light based on what the other measured.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them what a baud rate is. It is how fast the two boards agree to talk.
sessions.content: Getting two boards to talk to each other. A protocol is an agreed language, and UART is asynchronous — there is no shared clock, so the two devices simply agree in advance how fast to send, which is the baud rate. One Arduino reads a sensor, the other acts on the value.

sessions.title: I2C Protocol & Sensor Integration
keyConcepts: Reducing pin usage with I2C LCDs
activities: Display DHT22 data on an I2C LCD
sessions.task: Add LED/buzzer alerts for temperature ranges (cool/moderate/hot)
sessions.parentSummary: A second communication method that needs only two wires no matter how many devices are attached. Your child put a temperature sensor and a display on the same pair of wires.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask why saving pins on the board matters once a project gets big.
sessions.content: Reading a DHT sensor properly and putting the result on an LCD. The DHT11 covers a narrow range and suits simple projects; the DHT22 is wider and more accurate. The code checks each reading is valid before displaying it, because a failed read returns nothing rather than an error.

sessions.title: SPI Protocol
activities: Build a Master-Slave system: Send keypad input (Master) to LCD (Slave) via SPI
sessions.task: Investigate SPI daisy-chaining
sessions.parentSummary: A third protocol, faster than the last, with one device leading and the others following. Your child built a system where a keypad on one board writes to a screen on another.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them which of the three methods they would choose for a fast sensor, and why.
sessions.content: SPI, a second communication protocol and a faster one. It uses four wires — one for data out, one for data in, a clock line that tells both sides when to read, and a select line that picks which device is being addressed. The class implements it bit by bit rather than calling a library, so what the wires carry is visible.

sessions.title: PWM (Pulse Width Modulation)
activities: Control LED brightness with a potentiometer using PWM
sessions.task: Send potentiometer values between Arduinos via serial for remote PWM control
sessions.parentSummary: How a board that can only switch on and off produces something in between, by switching very fast. This is how dimmed lights and motor speed control actually work.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them how a light can be half on when the board only knows on and off.
sessions.content: Pulse width modulation: a digital pin can only be on or off, but switching it on and off fast enough makes it behave like something in between. The proportion of time it spends on is the duty cycle. Mapping converts a reading from one range to another, which is what lets a potentiometer's 0-1023 drive a 0-255 output.

sessions.title: EEPROM & Data Storage
activities: Create a password lock storing codes in EEPROM
Recover settings after power-off
sessions.task: Research EEPROM wear leveling
sessions.parentSummary: Memory that survives being unplugged. Your child built a password lock that still remembers its code after the power is cut.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Unplug their lock, plug it back in and check it still knows the password.
sessions.content: Memory that survives a power cut. EEPROM is storage on the chip itself that keeps its contents when the board is switched off — the difference between a robot that remembers its settings and one that forgets everything each time. Built into a digital code lock that keeps its code.

sessions.title: Interrupts
activities: Build an emergency pause system (button interrupt stops LED/buzzer)
Measure interrupt response time vs. polling
sessions.task: Identify interrupt use in smartphones (e.g., touchscreens)
sessions.parentSummary: Interrupts — how a device drops what it is doing to respond immediately. Your child built an emergency stop button and measured how much faster it responds than checking in a loop.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them why an emergency stop cannot afford to wait its turn.
sessions.content: Interrupts. Instead of the program checking a pin over and over, an interrupt lets the hardware tap the processor on the shoulder: it stops, runs a short handler, and returns to what it was doing. The session compares polling with interrupts and covers the modes — rising, falling and change.

sessions.title: Joystick & Servo Control
activities: Control dual servos with a joystick (pan-tilt mechanism)
sessions.task: Explore alternative movement sensors (e.g., accelerometers)
sessions.parentSummary: A joystick driving two servo motors, the pan-and-tilt mechanism used for cameras. Your child mapped the joystick's range onto the motors' range of movement.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to steer it for you and explain what happens when the stick is centred.
sessions.content: The joystick, which is two potentiometers at right angles plus a push switch. Each axis reports 0 to 1023 with the centre in the middle, and the two readings together drive two servo motors — the same arrangement as a game controller.

sessions.title: Graduation Project
sessions.steamTopic: How data is stored on the internet
sessions.parentSummary: The graduation project. Your child designs and builds something of their own using everything from the three levels, with the instructor supporting rather than directing.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask what they chose to build and why. This one is theirs.
sessions.content: The graduation project. Students choose what to build — a smart office, a calculator, a stopwatch or their own idea — then wire the components and write the code themselves, using everything from the three levels.

sessions.title: Introduction to AI
keyConcepts: Importance of AI in Our Lives
activities: Research and document real-world applications of AI
sessions.parentSummary: An introduction to what artificial intelligence actually is, where it already appears in daily life, and the idea that a machine can learn from examples rather than being told every rule. Your child also researched AI applications of their own choosing.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to point out three things in the house that use AI. The answers may surprise you.
sessions.content: What artificial intelligence is and where it already appears in daily life. Machine learning is introduced as a type of AI that learns from examples rather than from rules: you show the model many examples, then ask it to judge something it has not seen.

sessions.title: Fundamentals of Python for AI
activities: Build a working clock application in Python
sessions.parentSummary: A refresher on the Python your child needs for the rest of the course — variables, conditions, loops and functions — put to work building a working clock program.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to show you the clock running and explain what makes it update.
sessions.content: A refresher on the Python the rest of the course depends on — variables, conditions, loops and functions — including while loops and the infinite loop that repeats until something stops it.

sessions.title: Working with Data in AI
keyConcepts: Basic Info About DataFrames (head, tail, index, shape, columns, info, describe, sum, min, max, mean)
Dropping a Column from a DataFrame
activities: Build a Tic-Tac-Toe game with an AI opponent
sessions.parentSummary: The two libraries every AI project uses: one for handling large grids of numbers quickly, the other for working with tables of data. Your child also built a Tic-Tac-Toe game that plays against you.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Play their game and try to beat it.
sessions.content: The two libraries every AI project uses. NumPy handles large grids of numbers efficiently; Pandas analyses, cleans and explores datasets. Boolean indexing lets you select the rows of a dataset that satisfy a condition.

sessions.title: Supervised Learning
activities: Read the Titanic dataset from CSV
Explore the data with Pandas
Clean it: handle missing values and convert categorical data
Split into training and testing sets, fit a model and check its performance
sessions.parentSummary: The first real machine learning model. Your child used historical passenger data from the Titanic to build something that predicts who was likely to survive, working through the full process: read the data, examine it, train, test.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask what the model thinks would have happened to someone like you, and what it based that on.
sessions.content: The shape of a supervised learning problem. Classification predicts a discrete label — one of a set of categories; regression predicts a continuous number. Features come in the same two flavours, categorical and numeric, and the distinction decides which model can be used.

sessions.title: Unsupervised Learning
activities: Build a model predicting sales from advertising spend
Visualise the relationship between the variables
sessions.parentSummary: Learning without being given the answers. Your child built a model that predicts sales from advertising spend, and met overfitting — when a model memorises its examples instead of learning the pattern.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them what overfitting is. Revising by memorising past papers is the everyday version.
sessions.content: Learning without labels. Clustering groups data points by similarity to find structure nobody labelled in advance. The session also covers overfitting and underfitting — a model that has memorised its examples versus one that has not learned enough from them.

sessions.title: Introduction to Neural Networks
activities: Build a neural network that recognises handwritten digits from the MNIST dataset
sessions.steamTopic: RGB: how a computer represents colour
sessions.parentSummary: Neural networks. Your child built one that recognises handwritten digits, and learned how such a network is arranged in layers and how it corrects itself as it trains.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Write a number on paper, show it to their model, and see if it reads it correctly.
sessions.content: Neural networks and how they are trained. A network is arranged in layers, and a loss function acts as the judge, comparing each prediction with the true answer so the network can correct itself over many passes.

sessions.title: Vectors and Sequence Models
activities: Build a sequence model in TensorFlow
sessions.parentSummary: How text is turned into numbers so a machine can work with it, and models that handle sequences where order matters — the difference between a bag of words and a sentence.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask why “the dog bit the man” and “the man bit the dog” are hard for a computer to tell apart.
sessions.content: Turning text into numbers so a machine can work with it — mapping each word to a numerical representation — and sequence models, which handle data where the order carries meaning.

sessions.title: Natural Language Processing (NLP)
activities: Tokenize a text and score each word
Select the highest-scoring sentences to build a summary
sessions.steamTopic: How computers represent text in binary
sessions.parentSummary: Language processing: translation, question answering and summarising. Your child built a tool that takes a long piece of text and shortens it to the essentials.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Feed it a news article and see whether the summary is fair.
sessions.content: Natural language processing. Tokenization is the first step, breaking raw text into words or phrases the model can score. From there come the common tasks: classification, translation, question answering and summarising.

sessions.title: Training and Improving AI Models
activities: Download a dataset with TensorFlow's utilities
Train and evaluate a model on Stack Overflow data
sessions.steamTopic: Trial and error, and critical thinking
sessions.parentSummary: Why data is split into separate portions for training and testing, and why a model must never be examined on questions it has already seen. Your child worked with real data from Stack Overflow.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask why testing a model on its own training data is like marking your own homework.
sessions.content: Why data is split three ways — training, validation and testing — so a model is never judged on questions it has already seen. The session also introduces the deep learning layers that reduce and reshape data as it moves through a network.

sessions.title: Computer Vision
activities: Load a pre-trained YOLO v8 model
Run object detection on a photograph of your choice
sessions.parentSummary: Computer vision. Your child built a project that takes a photograph and identifies the objects in it, using a model already trained on millions of images.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Show it a photo from your phone and see what it finds.
sessions.content: Computer vision. Image classification says what an image contains; object detection goes further and locates each object, drawing a box around it. Pre-trained models let you use a network someone else trained on millions of images.

sessions.title: Motion and Image Understanding
activities: Build a project that identifies well-known people from photographs
sessions.parentSummary: Going further with images: separating an image into regions, estimating body position, and generating new images. Your child built a project that recognises well-known faces.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them what makes one face different from another as far as the computer is concerned.
sessions.content: Going further with images: separating a picture into regions, estimating the position of a body, and generating new images rather than only reading existing ones.

sessions.title: Ethics and the Future of AI
activities: Build a house price predictor from a Kaggle dataset
Examine the model for bias and unfairness
sessions.steamTopic: Reviewing the course, and whether AI can help
sessions.parentSummary: The level closes on ethics: bias, privacy, and who is accountable when an automated decision is wrong. Your child built a house price predictor and then examined it for unfairness.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them how an AI can end up being unfair without anyone intending it. This is the most important conversation in the course.
sessions.content: The ethics of automated decisions. Many AI systems are black boxes — data goes in, an answer comes out, and nobody can explain how it got there. That lack of transparency makes the decisions hard to trust and bias hard to detect.

sessions.title: Linear Regression and Prediction
activities: Create a small synthetic dataset by hand
Check for missing values
Visualise the relationship between the variables, then fit a regression model
sessions.steamTopic: The equation of a straight line
sessions.parentSummary: Level 2 starts by building a prediction model from scratch, with data your child entered by hand rather than downloaded. Building it manually makes clear what the library was doing for them in Level 1.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Give them a house size and let the model quote you a price.
sessions.content: Linear regression built from scratch. The goal is to find the line that best describes the relationship between the inputs and the value being predicted — the foundation the rest of the level builds on.

sessions.title: Error Analysis and Model Evaluation
activities: Rebuild the Titanic prediction with proper data cleaning
Measure how performance changes as model complexity rises
sessions.parentSummary: Why a model that scores well in training can still fail in the real world. Your child rebuilt the Titanic project and measured how performance changes as the model grows more complex.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask whether a more complicated model is always a better one. The answer is no, and they can explain why.
sessions.content: Why a model that scores well in training can still fail in the real world. Generalisation is the ability to perform on data never seen before, and cross-validation is how you estimate it honestly rather than fooling yourself with the training score.

sessions.title: Classification Logic and Boundaries
activities: Build a spam classifier from labelled email examples
Split the data and fit a linear model
sessions.parentSummary: How a model draws a line between two categories. Your child built a spam filter trained on labelled examples of real and unwanted email.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask what words make their filter suspicious of a message.
sessions.content: Classification as boundary drawing. A linear classifier separates categories with a line, and the decision boundary is what the model has actually learned. Contrasted with regression, which predicts a number rather than a class.

sessions.title: Evaluating Models and Class Imbalance
activities: Generate a dataset with deliberate class imbalance
Handle the imbalance, then build a model predicting whether a student passes
Evaluate it with a confusion matrix rather than accuracy alone
sessions.parentSummary: Measuring a model honestly. Your child built one that predicts whether a student will pass, then learned why accuracy alone can be misleading when one outcome is far more common than the other.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them how a model can be right 95% of the time and still be useless.
sessions.content: Measuring a model honestly. A confusion matrix breaks results into true and false positives and negatives, which matters when one outcome is far more common than the other — accuracy alone can look excellent while the model is useless.

sessions.title: Text Similarity and Feature Extraction
activities: Separate the words and strip punctuation
Build an unsupervised model comparing book reviews by similarity
sessions.parentSummary: Judging how similar two pieces of writing are, and the technique that decides which words in a document actually matter. Your child compared book reviews with it.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask why the word “the” tells you nothing about what a review is about.
sessions.content: Deciding how similar two pieces of writing are. Naive approaches — matching words, or comparing lengths — fail quickly, which motivates weighting words by how informative they are rather than how often they appear.

sessions.title: Classification in Real-World Contexts
activities: Load and explore a digits dataset
Classify handwritten digits from raw pixel values using KNN and a decision tree
sessions.steamTopic: How Google Maps finds the shortest path
sessions.parentSummary: Two more classification methods, including one that decides by looking at the closest examples it already knows. Your child used them to recognise handwritten digits from raw pixels.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to explain how a computer sees a handwritten 7 as a grid of numbers.
sessions.content: Two more classifiers. K-Nearest Neighbours decides by looking at the closest known examples. A decision tree works down from a root question through branches to an answer, which makes its reasoning readable in a way most models are not.

sessions.title: Clustering and Unsupervised Learning
activities: Load an image and explore its pixel data
Apply K-means to cluster the pixels into colour groups
Visualise the result
sessions.parentSummary: Grouping data without being told the groups in advance. Your child built a tool that reduces a photograph to its five main colours.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Run one of your photos through it and see which five colours it picks.
sessions.content: Clustering compared directly with classification: classification assigns items to categories you already defined, while clustering discovers the groups itself. K-means is the standard method, and the elbow method helps choose how many groups to look for.

sessions.title: Recommender Systems
activities: Build a popularity-based recommender
Add collaborative filtering, then content-based recommendation
Compare the three approaches
sessions.steamTopic: Graphs and why there are different kinds
sessions.parentSummary: How recommendation works — the machinery behind “you might also like”. Your child built a simple recommender and saw how it uses other people's choices to guess yours.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them how a streaming service decides what to suggest next.
sessions.content: How recommendation works. Popularity-based suggestions ignore the individual; collaborative filtering uses what similar people liked; content-based matching uses the properties of the item itself. A co-occurrence matrix records which things are liked together.

sessions.title: Robust Models and Outlier Impact
activities: Create and explore a dataset
Fit an SVM to classify different animals
sessions.steamTopic: Reading a change in performance from data
sessions.parentSummary: A method that copes better when data contains oddities and extremes. Your child used it to classify different animals.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask what a single strange example can do to a model that isn't built to resist it.
sessions.content: Support Vector Machines, which cope better when data contains extremes. Weights determine how much each feature counts towards the separation, so the model can give size more importance than colour when that is what distinguishes the classes.

sessions.title: Linear vs. Non-Linear Models
keyConcepts: Logistic Regression vs. KNN with Polynomial Features
activities: Create a dataset with a non-linear relationship
Fit a linear model, then a non-linear one
Compare their performance
sessions.parentSummary: Comparing straight-line models against ones that can bend, and when the extra flexibility is worth it. Your child built both and measured the difference.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them which performed better, and whether they expected that.
sessions.content: Straight lines are not always enough. When the relationship between the inputs and the answer curves, a linear model cannot capture it, and non-linear features are needed. The session builds both and measures the difference.

sessions.title: Ensemble Thinking & Decision Making
keyConcepts: Combining KNN, SVM, and Decision Trees for Better Accuracy
activities: Load and clean the data
Fit the combined model
Build a graphical interface that predicts a test result from symptoms
sessions.parentSummary: Combining several models so their mistakes cancel out. Your child built a diagnostic tool with a proper interface that predicts a test result from symptoms.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask why three imperfect models together can beat one good one.
sessions.content: Combining models so their individual weaknesses cancel out. KNN decides from nearby examples, an SVM draws the best boundary, and a decision tree reasons step by step — used together they outperform any of the three alone.

sessions.title: Final Graduation Project
activities: Design and build an AI project of your own
sessions.parentSummary: The graduation project: your child chooses a problem, picks the methods and builds the solution, with the instructor advising rather than directing.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask what they chose and why. This one is entirely theirs.
sessions.content: The graduation project. Students choose a problem, pick the methods and build the solution themselves, with the instructor advising rather than directing.

sessions.title: Genobot: meeting the EV3 kit
keyConcepts: The EV3 brick, sensors and motors
activities: Build the Genobot
Drive the motors straight from the brick buttons
sessions.task: Search about computer programming languages.
sessions.steamTopic: Robotics and the types of robots
sessions.parentSummary: The first session is about what a robot actually is and what is inside the EV3 kit. Your child sorted the parts into three groups — the sensors that gather information, the brick that decides what to do with it, and the motors that move — and built the Genobot to see all three working together.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask which parts of a washing machine are the sensors, which is the brain and which are the motors. The same three groups are in almost every machine at home.
sessions.content: What a robot is and the main families of them — autonomous mobile robots, humanoids and articulated arms. Then the EV3 kit itself, sorted into input, processing and output: the sensors that take information in, the brick that decides, and the motors that act. A motor is introduced as the part that turns electrical energy into movement.

sessions.title: Driving base: first program
activities: Build the driving base
Make the robot drive around the room in a square path
sessions.task: Search about mechanisms.
sessions.parentSummary: Your child moved from pressing buttons on the robot to writing a program for it. The class worked out how two motors together make a robot go straight or turn, then drove their robot around a square path — which needs the turns to be right, not just the driving.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to give you step-by-step instructions to walk a square around the room. Getting the turn wrong is exactly the bug they had to fix.
sessions.content: Programming languages, and why a robot needs instructions written in one. The session moves from pressing buttons on the brick to writing a sequence of blocks, and works through how the two motors combine: both forward drives straight, one forward and one back turns the robot on the spot.

sessions.title: Drawing bot: mechanisms
activities: Build the drawing bot
Program the motors to move and draw
sessions.task: Search about gears and their different types.
sessions.parentSummary: This session was about mechanisms — how machines change one kind of movement into another. Your child built a drawing robot, where a spinning motor is converted into a pen travelling across the paper.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Look at a bicycle together. The pedals go round, the wheels go round faster — the mechanism in between is what makes the difference.
sessions.content: Mechanisms — the arrangements of parts that turn one kind of movement into another — and the common types. The drawing bot applies it: a motor turns, and the mechanism converts that turning into a pen moving across paper.

sessions.title: Fan: gears and motor speed
activities: Build the fan
Set the speed of the motor and compare the results
sessions.task: Draw the types of gears.
sessions.parentSummary: Gears were the topic this week. Your child built a fan and changed both the gears and the speed set in the program, then compared what happened — the point being that speed and force trade against each other.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask why a bicycle has more than one gear. It is the same trade: easy pedalling or high speed, not both.
sessions.content: What gears are and what they are for. Gears change how fast something turns and how much force it turns with, and the fan build shows the effect directly: change the gear or change the programmed speed and the blades behave differently.

sessions.title: Gear shooter: types of gears
keyConcepts: Gear size and the effect on movement
activities: Build the gear shooter
Shoot different sizes of gear, measure which goes furthest and explain why
sessions.task: Research mathematical angles.
sessions.parentSummary: Your child built a launcher and used it as an experiment: fire gears of different sizes, see which travels furthest, then explain the result. Testing an idea rather than being told the answer is the habit being built here.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask what they found and why. If the explanation wobbles, that is fine — asking them to say it out loud is the exercise.
sessions.content: The different types of gears and what each is used for. The gear shooter turns it into an experiment: launch gears of different sizes, see which travels furthest, and work out why.

sessions.title: Driving base with the gyro sensor
keyConcepts: Turning by angle rather than by time
Using a reading to make a decision
activities: Build the driving base with a gyro sensor
Present what the gyro sensor did and how it was coded
sessions.task: Write down where electronic sensors are used in everyday life.
sessions.parentSummary: Sensors were the topic. Your child added a gyro sensor — which measures turning — so the robot could turn by an exact angle rather than by guessing how long to run the motors. They then explained their code to the group.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to name three sensors in your house. Automatic lights, a thermostat and a phone screen that rotates are all fair answers.
sessions.content: Sensors: what they measure and how a robot uses that reading to decide what to do next. The gyro sensor measures turning, so the driving base can be programmed to turn by a precise angle instead of guessing from time.

sessions.title: Gorilla: waiting for a sensor
keyConcepts: Reacting to the world instead of running a fixed sequence
activities: Build the gorilla
Code the colour and touch sensors so the robot moves only when it senses something
sessions.task: Practise what we have learned on the Scratch platform: https://scratch.mit.edu/projects/editor/?tutorial=getStarted
sessions.parentSummary: This week the robot learned to wait. Your child used a 'wait until' instruction so the gorilla stays still until its colour or touch sensor notices something — the difference between a robot that just performs and one that responds.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask what the robot was waiting for. Automatic doors work the same way: nothing happens until the sensor sees you.
sessions.content: Wait until — holding the program still until a sensor reports something, rather than running straight through. The gorilla build reacts only when the colour sensor or the touch sensor detects something, which is the difference between a robot that performs and a robot that responds.

sessions.title: Tracker: sensors and teamwork
activities: Build the tracker as a team
Put obstacles in front of it and use the sensors to get past them
sessions.task: Make a full presentation about the EV3 and its electronic components.
sessions.parentSummary: The last session of the level was a team build: a tracking robot that follows a line and uses its sensors to get around obstacles the class put in its way. Everything from the previous seven sessions had to be used at once.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to explain the EV3 parts to you as if you had never seen one. Their task this week is exactly that presentation.
sessions.content: The level closes with teamwork — dividing a build and a program between people — and the tracker, which follows a line and uses its sensors to deal with whatever is put in its way.

sessions.title: Free fall: gravity
keyConcepts: Controlling a falling part in code
activities: Build the free fall project
Control the falling part through the code
sessions.task: Search about the earth's gravitational force.
sessions.parentSummary: Level 2 opens with gravity — why things fall and what decides how fast. Your child built a free-fall model and controlled the falling part from code, so the physics and the programming meet in one project.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Drop a sheet of paper flat, then screwed into a ball. Ask why the ball wins when both weigh the same.
sessions.content: Gravitational force and the law behind it — why things fall, and why they fall the way they do. The free fall build lets students control the falling part from code and watch the effect.

sessions.title: Flower bot: if conditions
keyConcepts: Choosing between two paths in code
activities: Build the flower bot
Use an if condition to control it
sessions.task: Practise if conditions: https://studio.code.org/s/course3/lessons/7/levels/1
sessions.parentSummary: This session introduced the 'if' condition — code that checks something and then chooses what to do. Your child built a flower that opens and closes depending on what it senses.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to phrase a house rule as an if: 'if it is after eight, then…'. That is exactly the structure they coded.
sessions.content: The if condition — a program that checks something and takes a different path depending on the answer. The flower bot opens or closes depending on what it senses, which is a condition doing real work rather than a worksheet example.

sessions.title: Kickbox: gearing up and gearing down
keyConcepts: Planning a build across two sessions
activities: Build the kickbox ready for the next session
sessions.task: Set a proposal for the coding of the project.
sessions.parentSummary: Gearing was the topic: using gears to swap speed for strength, or the other way round. Your child started a kickbox build that is finished next session, so this week's homework is planning the code before writing any of it.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask what they are planning to make the kickbox do. Planning before building is the actual skill here.
sessions.content: Gearing up and gearing down — using gears to trade speed for force or force for speed. The kickbox build is started this session and finished the next, so the class has to plan the code before writing it.

sessions.title: Kickbox: the laws of motion
activities: Finish the kickbox
Program it to move its arms when it sees something
sessions.task: Make a presentation about types of gears, what they do and how they work.
sessions.parentSummary: Your child finished the kickbox and programmed it to swing when its sensor spots something. The session's science topic was the laws of motion, which is what the build demonstrates.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Their task is a presentation on gears. Ask for a two-minute version of it over dinner.
sessions.content: The laws of motion, and the kickbox finished and programmed. The robot is set to move its arms when it sees something, so the physics discussed at the start of the session is visible in what the build does.

sessions.title: Chicken: how birds fly
activities: Build the chicken
Practise the coding covered so far
sessions.task: Search about the types of link mechanisms.
sessions.parentSummary: This week looked at how birds fly, then built a mechanical chicken. Making a motor produce a walking, flapping movement is a harder problem than making it turn a wheel, which is the point of the build.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask how the chicken's legs move when the motor only goes round. The answer is the mechanism they built.
sessions.content: How birds fly, and the mechanism that reproduces the movement. The chicken build converts a motor's rotation into the flapping, stepping motion of an animal, which is a different problem from driving a wheel.

sessions.title: Biped walking robot: degrees of freedom
keyConcepts: Analysing a mechanism while building it
activities: Build the biped walking robot
Work out the degrees of freedom of the mechanism as you build
sessions.task: Search what kinematics is.
