sessions.steamTopic: Degrees of freedom of a mechanism
sessions.parentSummary: Your child built a two-legged walking robot and worked out its degrees of freedom — how many independent ways it can move. It is the idea engineers use to describe any mechanism, from a robot arm to a door hinge.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask how many ways a door can move, then an arm. A door has one; an arm has many. That is degrees of freedom.
sessions.content: Degrees of freedom — the number of independent ways a mechanism can move. A walking robot has to be understood this way before it can be built, so students guess the degrees of freedom of their own build as they assemble it.

sessions.title: Phone holder: kinematics
keyConcepts: Designing a build before coding it
activities: Build the phone holder ready for the next session
sessions.task: Make a presentation about dynamic and static mechanisms.
sessions.parentSummary: Kinematics — the study of how things move — was the topic. Your child began a phone holder build that is finished next session, and was asked to think about it as a mechanism before touching any code.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask for the difference between something that moves and something that holds still. That is the static versus dynamic distinction in their task.
sessions.content: Kinematics — describing movement in terms of position, speed and the path taken, without worrying about the forces behind it. The phone holder is started this session and completed the next, with the build planned as a mechanism first.

sessions.title: Phone holder: finishing and presenting
keyConcepts: Finishing a project to a deadline
activities: Finish the phone holder as a group, with each student coding one part
Present what you learned across the course
sessions.parentSummary: The final session was a group finish: the phone holder completed with each student responsible for one part of the code, then everyone presented what they had learned across the whole course.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask which project across the two levels they were proudest of, and why.
sessions.content: The level closes by finishing the phone holder as a group, with parts of the code assigned to different students, and each presenting what they learned across the course.

sessions.title: Dart and the first program
activities: Say hello to Flutter in DartPad
Print your name, age and favourite app
sessions.task: Write three differences between Flutter and native development.
sessions.parentSummary: The course opened with why apps are built the way they are: writing an app twice, once for Android and once for iPhone, or writing it once in Flutter. Your child wrote their first Dart program — printing their name and age to the screen.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask what Dart is and why Flutter needs it. The short answer: it is the language the app is written in.
sessions.content: What mobile app development is, and the choice between building an app twice — once in Kotlin for Android, once in Swift for iOS — or once in Flutter for both. Flutter's language is Dart, so the session ends in DartPad: every program starts at main(), print() puts a message on screen, and every instruction ends in a semicolon.

sessions.title: Loops and conditions in Dart
activities: Build a multiplication table generator
Build a number filter
sessions.task: Create a loop that prints even numbers from 1 to 20.
sessions.parentSummary: Loops and decisions. Your child learned the three ways Dart repeats something, and how a program chooses between paths with if and else, then built a multiplication table generator that uses both.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to count down from ten as a loop rather than ten separate instructions. That is the whole idea.
sessions.content: Loops — telling the computer to repeat something rather than writing it out ten times — in their three Dart forms: for, while and do-while. Alongside them the comparison operators and conditional statements, so a program can both repeat and decide.

sessions.title: Functions, parameters and lists
activities: Build a basic calculator in DartPad
sessions.task: Write a function that returns a welcome message using a name.
sessions.parentSummary: Functions were the topic: naming a chunk of code so it can be used again with different values instead of being rewritten. Your child built a working calculator out of them.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask what a function's 'parameter' is. A recipe that takes any number of people is the same idea.
sessions.content: Functions: naming a piece of code so it can be reused, passing values in as parameters, and returning a value back out. Dart's named and optional parameters are covered, along with arrow functions for short logic, and lists for holding several values under one name.

sessions.title: Object oriented programming in Dart
activities: Create a Book class in Dart
sessions.task: Create and print the details of two objects.
sessions.parentSummary: This session was about classes: writing one blueprint — say, for a book — and then making as many books from it as you like, each with its own title and author. It is how larger apps are kept organised.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask for the difference between 'a car' and 'your car'. That is a class and an object.
sessions.content: Classes and objects. A class is a blueprint — it says what properties and behaviours something has — and an object is one thing built from that blueprint. Constructors run automatically when an object is created and set it up, including named constructors and required named parameters.

sessions.title: Building a screen with rows and columns
activities: Build an 'All About Me' screen with text, a button and containers of fun facts
sessions.task: Add a text, a button and an image to your screen.
sessions.parentSummary: Your child moved from code output to an actual screen, arranging text, buttons and images in rows and columns. They built an 'All About Me' page as their first real interface.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Open any app and ask what is a row and what is a column. Almost every screen is made of the two.
sessions.content: Laying out a screen. Rows and columns arrange widgets across or down, and their properties decide the rest: main axis alignment for where items sit, spacing between and around them, expansion and flex for how leftover space is shared, and padding and alignment inside each box.

sessions.title: Navigating between screens
keyConcepts: Passing a choice from one screen to the next
activities: Build a two-screen pet info app: choose a pet, then see its picture and a fact
sessions.task: Add a return button and an animation between the pages.
sessions.parentSummary: An app is more than one screen, so this session was about moving between them. Your child built a pet app: pick a dog or a cat on the first screen, see its picture and a fact on the second.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask what the back button actually does. Flutter stacks screens on top of each other and back removes the top one.
sessions.content: Moving between screens. A button is what triggers navigation: pick the trigger, choose the action, and the app moves to another page and back again. The pet app is two screens, so the connection between them is the point of the build.

sessions.title: Setting up a real Flutter project
keyConcepts: flutter create and the project folder
activities: Install the tools and set up an emulator
Create and run your first Flutter project locally
sessions.task: Draw your Flutter folder structure.
sessions.parentSummary: Your child set up a proper development environment on the laptop — the Flutter toolkit, a code editor and a phone emulator — and ran their first project outside the drag-and-drop builder. Fiddly, and a real milestone.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to show you the emulator: a phone running on the laptop screen. It usually gets a good reaction.
sessions.content: Leaving the drag-and-drop builder for a real development environment: the Flutter SDK, an editor — VS Code or Android Studio, with the trade-offs of each — and an emulator to run on. The session also covers what a Flutter project folder actually contains.

sessions.title: Widgets in code: Scaffold, AppBar and buttons
activities: Build a Settings app with a Scaffold, an AppBar and a welcome message
Add buttons to it
sessions.task: Make the 'Change Text' button update the text on screen.
sessions.parentSummary: Your child wrote by hand what the builder had been generating: the page frame, the bar at the top, the buttons. The code words 'extends' and 'override' were explained here — they are how one widget builds on another.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask what a widget is. In Flutter, everything on screen is one — text, a button, even the spacing.
sessions.content: The same screens as before, now written by hand. Scaffold provides the page structure and AppBar the bar across the top. The session explains what extends and @override mean — inheriting from StatelessWidget and replacing its build method — and how a button's onPressed, child and style properties work.

sessions.title: Stateless and stateful widgets
activities: Build a counter app with plus and minus buttons
sessions.task: Convert a simple StatelessWidget into a StatefulWidget and use setState() so it responds to button clicks.
sessions.steamTopic: What is state in an app?
sessions.parentSummary: The idea this session was state: the difference between a screen that never changes and one that remembers something. Your child built a counter with plus and minus buttons, which is the smallest app that has to remember anything.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask what the app 'remembers'. Just the number — but that is state, and every app is built on it.
sessions.content: Why some widgets never change and others do. A stateless widget draws once; a stateful widget holds a value that can change, and setState() tells Flutter to redraw when it does. Checkboxes, sliders, forms and text fields are all stateful for this reason.

sessions.title: Forms, text fields and validation
activities: Build a login form with a username field, a password field and a login button
sessions.task: Show an error message if the password is shorter than six characters.
sessions.steamTopic: Password fields and why passwords are hidden
sessions.parentSummary: Your child built a login form and made it check its own input — refusing a password shorter than six characters and saying why. Validating input before trusting it is a habit worth having early.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask why the password is shown as dots. Then ask what happens if you type a short one into their app.
sessions.content: Taking input from the user. A TextField has a controller that holds what was typed, decoration for its label and border, obscureText for passwords and a keyboard type. A validator checks the input before the app accepts it, and navigation moves the user on once it passes.

sessions.title: Saving data with Firebase
activities: Build a notes app that saves a note to the cloud and displays it
sessions.task: Save a note and display it.
sessions.parentSummary: Until now everything the app knew disappeared when it closed. This session connected the app to cloud storage, so your child's notes app saves what you type and still has it next time.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask where the note goes when they press save. 'A computer somewhere else' is exactly right.
sessions.content: Storing data somewhere other than the phone. Firebase is initialised before the app starts, then data is written to and read from the cloud. The session compares FutureBuilder, which fetches once, with StreamBuilder, which keeps listening and rebuilds the screen whenever the data changes.

sessions.title: Final project: build your own app
keyConcepts: Choosing and scoping your own project
activities: Build your own app from your own idea
sessions.task: Present your app: what it does, how you designed it, what you learned and what problems you solved.
sessions.parentSummary: The final session was your child's own app, chosen by them and built from everything in the level, then presented to the group — including what went wrong and how they fixed it.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask for the demo. Ask what they would add if they had another two weeks.
sessions.content: The level closes with an app of the student's own choosing, built from everything covered — layout, navigation, state, forms and Firebase — and then presented: what it does, how it was designed, what was learned and which problems had to be solved.

sessions.title: Responsive layouts
activities: Build a profile card app that works in both portrait and landscape
sessions.task: Change the name, photo, about-me text and hobbies to your own, then rotate the screen and check it still looks right.
sessions.steamTopic: Responsive versus adaptive versus fluid design
sessions.parentSummary: Level 2 opens on a real problem: phones come in many sizes. Your child built a profile card that still looks right when the phone is turned sideways, using layout rules rather than fixed positions.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Rotate your own phone in a few apps. Some handle it well and some do not — that is exactly what this session was about.
sessions.content: Making one app look right on many screen sizes. Responsive, adaptive and fluid design are distinguished, then applied with SafeArea to keep content clear of notches and bars, and Expanded and Flexible to share space instead of fixing it.

sessions.title: Stacking widgets on top of each other
activities: Build a poster maker: an image with text placed on top of it
sessions.task: Change the poster image and message, move the text around, and make your own poster.
sessions.parentSummary: This session was about layering — putting text on top of an image instead of next to it. Your child built a poster maker and could drag the text anywhere over the picture.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to make you a poster in it. Layering is how every meme and every film title works.
sessions.content: Layering. Stack places widgets on top of one another and Positioned decides exactly where each sits, which is how text goes over an image rather than beside it.

sessions.title: Bottom navigation and drawers
keyConcepts: Switching pages without leaving the screen
activities: Build a mini social app with Home, Profile and Settings pages
sessions.task: Rename the pages, add more items to the drawer, and change what the logout action does.
sessions.parentSummary: Your child built an app with three sections and a bar along the bottom to switch between them — the layout almost every app on your phone uses.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Count the tabs along the bottom of a favourite app. That is the widget they built this week.
sessions.content: Apps with several main sections. A BottomNavigationBar switches between them along the bottom of the screen, and a Drawer slides in from the side for everything that does not fit there.

sessions.title: Grids and cards
keyConcepts: Choosing how many items per row
activities: Build a photo gallery of six to nine photos, each in a card
sessions.task: Add more photos, change how many appear per row, open an image full screen when tapped, and add captions.
sessions.steamTopic: How Facebook and YouTube handle billions of likes and views
sessions.parentSummary: Your child built a photo gallery laid out in a grid, much like the picture apps on your phone. The extension task was making a photo open full screen when you tap it.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask how the gallery knows how many photos fit per row. It is a setting, and they changed it.
sessions.content: Showing many items at once. A grid arranges items in rows and columns that reflow with the screen, and a Card gives each one its own raised, rounded surface.

sessions.title: Animation basics
activities: Build a magic box that changes colour, size and position every time it is tapped, with a message that fades in and out
sessions.task: Add a second text widget below the first that fades in and out the same way.
sessions.parentSummary: Animation this week — and specifically why apps use it: a change that slides instead of jumping tells you what happened. Your child built a box that changes colour, size and position each time it is tapped.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to show you the magic box. Then ask why a jump would feel worse than a slide.
sessions.content: Why apps animate — to feel alive, and to show the user what just happened. AnimatedContainer changes size, colour and position smoothly rather than jumping; opacity and alignment animate the same way.

sessions.title: Hero and tween animations
activities: Build a movie app where tapping a poster makes it fly to the detail screen
sessions.task: Add a second TweenAnimationBuilder on the detail page to fade the movie title in below the poster.
sessions.parentSummary: Your child built a film app where tapping a poster makes it fly across into the next screen. It is the same trick the app store uses when you tap an app icon.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Tap an app in the store and watch the icon expand into the page. Ask if they can see how theirs does the same.
sessions.content: Two more kinds of animation and the difference between them: a Hero animation carries an element from one screen to the next so it appears to fly across, while a TweenAnimationBuilder animates a value between a start and an end.

sessions.title: Lists and search
keyConcepts: Filtering a list as the user types
activities: Build a contacts app with a scrolling list of names and icons
sessions.task: Add a search bar so that typing filters the list to matching names.
sessions.parentSummary: Your child built a contacts list — a scrolling list built from data rather than typed out one by one — and then added a search box that filters it as you type.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask what happens to the other names when you search. They are still there; the app just stops showing them.
sessions.content: Displaying a list of data on screen rather than in the console. Dart lists are revisited, then turned into a scrolling list of rows in the app, and a search box filters it as the user types.

sessions.title: Forms: switches, checkboxes and dropdowns
activities: Build a survey app with switches, checkboxes and dropdowns, plus a summary page
sessions.task: After submitting, show a new screen with all the answers, and add a smooth transition to it.
sessions.steamTopic: The difference between forms and surveys
sessions.parentSummary: Your child built a survey app using switches, tick boxes and dropdown menus, then a summary screen showing everything the user picked — which is how every form you fill in online is put together.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to survey the family with it. Choosing the right control for each question is the design decision.
sessions.content: The rest of the input controls. Switches, checkboxes and dropdown menus each collect a different kind of answer, and a summary page shows the user what they chose before anything is submitted.

sessions.title: Tabs and swipe navigation
activities: Build a news app with Sports, Technology and Fun Zone tabs
sessions.task: Add a fourth Science tab with its own page and three articles, using the same card layout.
sessions.parentSummary: Your child built a news app with tabs across the top that you can also swipe between, each holding its own set of articles.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to add a tab for something they care about. The task this week is exactly that.
sessions.content: Tabs: several categories along the top of a screen, switched by tapping or by swiping sideways, with each tab holding its own scrolling content.

sessions.title: Authentication: sign up and sign in
keyConcepts: Sign up and sign in screens
activities: Build an authentication app with sign up, sign in and home screens
sessions.task: Add a logout button that returns to the login screen, and a login link on the sign-up screen for users who already have an account.
sessions.parentSummary: Your child built the sign-up and sign-in screens that almost every app starts with, and wired them together — including what happens when you log out.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask why an app needs both a sign-up screen and a sign-in screen. It is a question a lot of first-time builders get wrong.
sessions.content: A complete authentication flow across three screens: sign up with email and password, sign in, and the home screen you reach once you are in — plus the links between them.

sessions.title: Putting the app together
activities: Assemble the screens from the level into one structured app
sessions.task: Add an item description screen: tapping an item in the favourites list opens a screen showing its details.
sessions.parentSummary: This session was about structure — how the screens built over the level fit together into one app, and where everything belongs. The class also looked at GitHub, which is how developers keep and share their code.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask what GitHub is for. 'Saving your work so you can go back' is a good enough answer.
sessions.content: Structuring a full app rather than a single screen: how the pieces built over the level fit into one project, and where each screen and each piece of data belongs.

sessions.title: Final project and presentations
activities: Present your app to the group
sessions.task: Present your app: what it does, how you designed it, what you learned and what problems you solved.
sessions.parentSummary: The last session was presentations: each student showed their app, explained how they designed it and what they had to work out along the way. The group also talked about how AI is changing what apps can do.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask for the presentation at home too. Explaining your own work is half the skill.
sessions.content: The course closes with each student presenting their own app — what it does, how it was designed, what they learned and what they had to solve — and a look at where mobile development is going with AI.

sessions.title: What programming is
activities: Complete the introductory blocks activity
Research machine code, the language computers actually run
sessions.task: Do research about the language of computers and what is machine code. Write down the blocks from level 7 to 14
sessions.parentSummary: The very beginning: what a program actually is, and why we start with coloured blocks instead of typing. Your child also looked into how computers understand instructions underneath it all.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them what machine code is. It is the language the computer really speaks.
sessions.content: Programming is the process of creating a set of instructions that tell a computer how to perform a task. The session covers what can be built with it, and why we start with coloured blocks rather than typed code.

sessions.title: Sequencing and algorithms
activities: Write out the steps for making a pizza as an algorithm
Complete the drag-and-drop blocks activity
sessions.task: Drag the food or the toy to the pet and watch the sprites interact. Write down the blocks from level 5 to 11
sessions.parentSummary: Order matters. Your child learned that a computer does exactly what it is told in exactly the order given, and that a recipe of steps has a name: an algorithm.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to give you instructions for brushing your teeth, then follow them far too literally.
sessions.content: Sequencing, and the discovery that computers and people do not understand requests the same way. A computer needs every step spelled out in order — which is what an algorithm is.

sessions.title: Finding and fixing mistakes
activities: Debug the broken block programs
Play the logic gates quiz game
sessions.task: Play this baamboozle game about logic gates. Debug the blocks from level 5 to 11
sessions.parentSummary: Debugging — this session was about programs that are broken on purpose, so your child gets used to reading code and working out what went wrong.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them how they find a mistake in a program. Guessing is not the method they were taught.
sessions.content: Logic gates, the building blocks of digital circuits, which perform the basic logical operations every computer depends on. Illustrated with examples from Super Mario, then applied to finding and fixing broken block programs.

sessions.title: Events
activities: Build a game on code.org using events
Add a rainbow background and a new sprite
sessions.task: Put a background rainbow. put a new sprite
sessions.parentSummary: Making a program respond to something happening — a click, a key press. Until now programs ran straight through; now they wait and react.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to show you what happens when you press a key in their project.
sessions.content: Events: making a program respond to something happening rather than running straight through. Introduced through classical conditioning — training a pet to react to a signal — before applying the same idea in code.

sessions.title: Loops
activities: Solve each puzzle using only one or two blocks
Add a sprite that repeats ten times in a random position
sessions.task: The project is the same as before. Add a new sprite repeat it 10 times and make the location random
sessions.parentSummary: Repetition. Instead of placing the same block ten times, your child learned to tell the program to repeat it, and added a character that appears in a random position each run.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask why the character lands somewhere different every time.
sessions.content: Loops, and why repeating a block ten times is worse than telling the program to repeat it. The session pushes students to solve the same puzzle in fewer and fewer blocks.

sessions.title: Working in pairs, and better loops
activities: Build an ocean scene using loops
Research how loops are used in block code
sessions.task: Research loops and advanced loops and how we use them in block code. Write down the blocks from level 1 to 5
sessions.parentSummary: More advanced repetition, and pair programming — two people, one keyboard, taking turns. Explaining your thinking out loud is a real programming skill.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask what it was like to code with a partner, and whether it helped.
sessions.content: Pair programming, where one student navigates and keeps the big picture while the other drives and handles the detail, then they swap. Alongside it, more advanced loops for building repeating scenes.

sessions.title: Sprites
activities: Build a swimming fish project in Sprite Lab
Make a sprite say 'Hello world'
sessions.task: The project is the same as before Make the sprite say “Hello world”
sessions.parentSummary: Sprites are the characters on screen. Your child learned to create them, move them and make them speak.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to make a sprite say something to you.
sessions.content: Sprites in Sprite Lab: a graphic with a location, size and appearance, and behaviours — actions a sprite performs continuously until told to stop.

sessions.title: Data and binary
keyConcepts: Research binary language and how we use it
activities: Chart a set of collected data
Research binary and how computers use it
sessions.parentSummary: How computers store everything as ones and zeros. Your child researched binary and saw how letters become numbers before they become electricity.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to write your initial in binary.
sessions.content: Data and how it is represented. Collecting and graphing data lets you ask and answer questions you could not otherwise — the example is whether goals are scored more often from the left or the right.

sessions.title: Variables
keyConcepts: Make a variable called age and put the age from math blocks
activities: Build a project with a city background and a new sprite
Create an age variable and set it from the maths blocks
sessions.parentSummary: A variable is a labelled box that holds a value the program can change. Your child made one to store an age and used it in a project.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them what a variable is. A box with a name on it is the answer they were given.
sessions.content: Variables, explained as containers: when someone types into a prompt, the computer stores what they typed in a labelled container, and the label says what kind of information to expect.

sessions.title: Conditionals
keyConcepts: The project is the same as before
Use the if statement to check to the person if he can vote or not
activities: Use an if statement to check whether a person is old enough to vote
sessions.parentSummary: Programs that make decisions. Your child built one that checks an age and works out whether that person is old enough to vote.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to run it with your age, then with theirs.
sessions.content: Conditionals: a program that checks something and takes a different path depending on the answer. Applied to a real decision with a clear rule.

sessions.title: Functions
keyConcepts: Play a bamboozle game about functions
activities: Play the functions quiz game
Debug the broken programs
sessions.parentSummary: Grouping a set of blocks under one name so it can be reused, plus more practice hunting bugs.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask why writing the same code three times is a bad idea.
sessions.content: Functions, which group a set of blocks under one name so they can be reused, plus more practice finding bugs in programs that do not behave as intended.

sessions.title: Choosing the right tool
activities: Present your favourite project from the level
sessions.parentSummary: The level closes by looking at which app or tool suits which job — a genuine skill, and a good moment to look back over everything built this term.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to show you their favourite project from the level.
sessions.content: Choosing the right tool for the job, and a review of everything built across the level — a genuine skill, since the same project can be easy or painful depending on what it is built in.

sessions.title: How a computer works
activities: Build a game with a scoring variable
Research the different types of computer
sessions.task: Add water to the background Please create a new fish sprite Create a variable named "score" and assign it a value of zero using the math blocks
sessions.parentSummary: Level 2 opens by looking inside the machine — what the parts do and how instructions actually run — then straight back into building, with a scoring system in a game.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to name the main parts of a computer and what each one is for.
sessions.content: How a computer works: the parts inside it, what each one does, and how instructions actually run. The level opens by looking inside the machine before building anything with it.

sessions.title: Problem solving
activities: Work through the Hourglass Time puzzle
Research the inputs and outputs of a computer
sessions.task: Make a research about inputs and outputs of computer
sessions.parentSummary: Breaking a large problem into pieces small enough to solve. This is the habit the whole course is built around, and it applies well beyond programming.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Give them a big task, like tidying a room, and ask them to break it into steps.
sessions.content: The problem-solving process as four steps: define what you are solving and what success looks like, plan an approach, try it, then reflect on what could be done better. It applies well beyond programming.

sessions.title: Inputs, outputs and loops
activities: Build a Dance Party project using events
Draw a repeating pattern with loops
sessions.task: Add water to the background Please create a new fish sprite Create a variable named "score" and assign it a value of zero using the math blocks Draw a small yellow ball and insert it as a new sprite and make it repeat 5 times
sessions.parentSummary: Everything a computer does is something in, something out. Your child mapped that idea onto their projects and combined it with events and loops.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to list the inputs and outputs of a games console.
sessions.content: Input is the information a computer receives from people, devices or other computers; output is what it gives back. Everything a program does sits between the two. Combined with events and loops in a dance party project.

sessions.title: Variables and functions
activities: Build an artist project driven by variables
Research why data matters
sessions.task: Play this bamboozle game about the solar system
sessions.parentSummary: Storing information and packaging up reusable pieces of a program — the two ideas that stop projects becoming unmanageable as they grow.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them what would happen without variables. Everything would have to be written out by hand.
sessions.content: How information is stored. A bit is a single piece of binary information, the binary system represents anything using only two options, and ASCII is the agreed system for turning text into those numbers. Variables are introduced as the containers that hold it.

sessions.title: Loops and functions together
activities: Build the nectar-picking loop project
Write a 'build a bridge' function and call it
sessions.task: Add the space to the background Please create three new alien sprites Make the first one spin to the left Make the second one growing Make the third one spin to the right
sessions.parentSummary: Combining repetition with reusable blocks in a space-themed project, with three characters each behaving differently.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to show you the project and explain why each character moves the way it does.
sessions.content: For loops — repeating a set of instructions a fixed number of times — used together with functions, which name a group of steps so they can be called again rather than rebuilt.

sessions.title: The design process
activities: Present a summary of the previous five sessions
sessions.task: Please provide a summary presentation of the last five sessions
sessions.parentSummary: How designers work: plan, build, test, improve. Your child also presented a summary of everything from the last five sessions, which is harder than it sounds.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to give you their presentation. Explaining something is the best test of understanding it.
sessions.content: The design process: a series of steps for arriving at a solution, starting from empathy — choosing what to build based on what a user actually needs rather than what is easy to make.

sessions.title: Designing for the person using it
activities: Categorise your users and brainstorm solutions for each group
Build a PictoBlox project with a sky backdrop and a talking sprite
sessions.task: Put the backdrop blue sky Please create a new sprite Make the sprite say “Hello world” for  3 Seconds Change the backdrop using blocks
sessions.parentSummary: Thinking about the person who will use the program rather than the person writing it. A good program is one that makes sense to someone who was not there when it was built.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Use one of their projects without instructions and tell them what confused you.
sessions.content: User-centred design and design thinking. Students group their users into categories, then brainstorm solutions aimed at a specific kind of person rather than an imaginary average one.

sessions.title: Feedback and testing
activities: Redesign a screen based on feedback received
Build a PictoBlox project with movement and sound
sessions.task: Make Tobi say “You’re the best programmer” Swipe it to the left Play a sound until it done
sessions.parentSummary: Testing properly, and taking feedback without treating it as criticism. Your child improved a project based on what other people found.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask what someone else suggested and whether they agreed with it.
sessions.content: Feedback and testing. Students sort the feedback they receive into categories, then each redesigns one screen based on one improvement and sketches what the new interface would look like.

sessions.title: Codes and secret messages
activities: Invent a rule that can represent any word using the available symbols
Encode and decode a message with it
sessions.parentSummary: How text becomes numbers and numbers become binary, and how messages can be encoded and decoded. Children usually love this one.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to send you a message in code and make you work it out.
sessions.content: Patterns and representation: inventing a rule that lets you encode any word using a limited set of symbols. Students design the rule themselves, which is what a character encoding actually is.

sessions.title: How images are stored
activities: Recover a scrambled image by correcting its width and height
Research why keeping your data private matters
sessions.parentSummary: A picture is a grid of coloured dots, and each colour is a number. Your child learned how a photograph is stored as pure data.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them how a phone stores a photo. There are no pictures inside, only numbers.
sessions.content: How images are stored. A picture is a grid of pixels, and its width and height decide how those pixels are arranged — set them wrongly and the image is unrecognisable, which is what the pixelation widget demonstrates.

sessions.title: Putting representations together
activities: Build a student record combining several kinds of data
Research what AI is
sessions.task: Make a decryption to your name using pictoblox
sessions.parentSummary: Combining text, numbers and images as different kinds of stored data, including writing their own name as an encoded message.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to decode something for you.
sessions.content: Combining representations: a single record holds text, numbers and yes/no answers together. The session uses a student record to show how much can be inferred from data, and why keeping some of it secret matters.

sessions.title: Machine learning
activities: Train a model to recognise fish by their features
Build a project on code.org that tells cats from dogs
sessions.task: Make a project using code.org to make the A.I. detect the difference between the cat and the dog
sessions.parentSummary: The level ends with a first taste of AI: your child trained a program to tell cats from dogs by showing it examples rather than writing rules.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Show it a photo it hasn't seen and see whether it gets it right.
sessions.content: A first look at machine learning: training a program by showing it examples rather than writing rules, then inspecting which features it is actually using to decide.

sessions.title: Problem solving with PictoBlox
activities: Make Tobi move five steps and turn 50 degrees left
Use a loop to make Tobi say hello five times
sessions.task: Make Tobi move 5 steps Also make it turn to the left 50 degrees Use a loop to make Tobi say  “hello” five times
sessions.parentSummary: Level 3 begins with a review of movement, turning and loops in PictoBlox before the term moves on to building websites.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to make their character walk in a square. It needs a loop and a turn.
sessions.content: The level opens on problem solving, revisiting movement, turning and loops in PictoBlox before the term moves on to building for the web.

sessions.title: Building a calculator
activities: Build a simple calculator with the four operations
Research how a computer works in terms of input, processing and output
sessions.task: Make a simple calculator Put these operators only ( + , - , * , /) Put a button to take the numbers Put another button to get the result
sessions.parentSummary: A working calculator with the four operations and buttons to drive it. It brings together input, processing and output in one project.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to add something up on their own calculator.
sessions.content: The kinds of processing a computer does: comparing two things, counting how many there are, and if/then decisions. Together these are the operations behind every program students have written so far.

sessions.title: How web pages work
activities: Present the process of building a web page with HTML
sessions.task: Create a presentation on the process of building a webpage with HTML
sessions.parentSummary: The first look at the web: what a page is made of and how a browser turns code into something you can read. Your child presented the process of building one.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them what happens between typing an address and the page appearing.
sessions.content: How a web page is put together. The head holds metadata meant for search engines and other programs; the body holds everything a person actually sees.

sessions.title: Building with HTML
activities: Build a restaurant website with HTML
sessions.task: Create the website of your restaurant from what you learned using HTML
sessions.parentSummary: Your child wrote their first real web page — a restaurant site — using HTML, the language that gives a page its structure.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to open their restaurant page and show you the code behind it.
sessions.content: Filling in the body: text, images, tables, forms and headings — everything designed for human eyes. Built in pairs, with one student navigating and the other typing.

sessions.title: Styling with CSS
activities: Restyle the restaurant website with CSS
sessions.task: Edit the website of your restaurant from what you learned today using HTML
sessions.parentSummary: HTML decides what is on a page; CSS decides how it looks. Your child restyled their restaurant site. We also talked about intellectual property and using other people's work fairly.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them why you cannot simply take any image off the internet for your own site.
sessions.content: CSS, which decides how a page looks while HTML decides what is on it. A rule targets an element and sets its properties. The session also covers intellectual property and using other people's work fairly.

sessions.title: Drawing with code
activities: Complete the drawing challenge
Present the steps involved in building a professional website
sessions.task: Please create a presentation that outlines the steps involved in creating a professional website with a focus on functional concepts
sessions.parentSummary: Producing shapes and patterns by writing instructions rather than drawing by hand, plus a presentation on what makes a website professional.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to draw you something using only code.
sessions.content: How computer science is used in entertainment, then drawing by instruction — producing shapes and patterns in code rather than by hand.

sessions.title: Shapes, parameters and Scratch
activities: Work out how the same code produced differently sized rectangles
Research what a variable is and give an example
sessions.task: Create a snake game project using code.org
sessions.parentSummary: Giving a reusable block different values each time it runs, so one instruction can draw many different shapes. Your child also started a Snake game.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask how one block can draw both a triangle and a hexagon.
sessions.content: Parameters: giving a reusable block a different value each time it runs, so one instruction can draw many different shapes rather than one fixed shape.

sessions.title: Random numbers and sprites
activities: Create a sprite and animate it
Build a Snake game
Research random numbers in programming
sessions.task: Use code.org's Sprite Lab project to bring your imagination to life and create your very own game!
sessions.parentSummary: Randomness makes a game different every time it is played. Your child used it to build a game of their own design.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Play their game twice and ask why it wasn't the same.
sessions.content: Sprites in Game Lab, and dot notation — connecting a sprite to one of its properties with a dot to read or change it. Random numbers make a game different every time it is played.

sessions.title: Sprite games
activities: Predict where the bee sprite will appear, then test the prediction
Build a fish game where big fish eat small fish
sessions.task: Create a fish game using code.org's Sprite Lab where big fish eat small fish
sessions.parentSummary: A fish game where bigger fish eat smaller ones, which needs collision detection and size comparison — more logic than it first appears.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Play it and ask how the game knows when one fish has caught another.
sessions.content: Sprite properties in practice: predicting where a sprite will appear from the code alone, before running it. Predicting output is how you check you understand a program rather than guessing at it.

sessions.title: Programming languages
activities: Present programming languages and what each is used for
sessions.task: Create a presentation on programming languages and their respective applications
sessions.parentSummary: Why there are so many programming languages and what each is good at. Your child presented their findings.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them which language they would use to build a website, and which for a game.
sessions.content: What programming actually is — giving a set of instructions to a computer, the way a recipe gives instructions to a cook — and why there are so many programming languages, each suited to different work.

sessions.title: First steps in Python
activities: Write a Python program that prints your name and age
sessions.task: Make a program using Python to write your name and your age
sessions.parentSummary: The move from coloured blocks to typed code. Your child wrote their first Python program — printing their name and age — and met variables and data types in text form.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask how typing code compares with dragging blocks. Most children find it harder but more satisfying.
sessions.content: The move from coloured blocks to typed code. Python's rules for naming a variable: no spaces, no starting with a number, no special characters except the underscore, and no reusing a name already in use.

sessions.title: Innovations in computing
activities: Choose a field and present how computing could improve it
Present machine learning and its applications
sessions.task: Please create a presentation on the topic of machine learning and its applications for computers
sessions.parentSummary: The course closes by looking outward: machine learning, where computing is heading, and what your child might want to learn next.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask what they want to build next. This is the moment to find out.
sessions.content: How computing is changing other fields, from farming to wearable technology, and where students might take it next. The course closes by looking outward rather than at more syntax.

sessions.title: Variables and input
keyConcepts: What’s programming language and what is python used for
activities: Store three animal names in separate variables and print them
Calculate the area of a shape from fixed values, then from user input
sessions.task: Ask the user to enter the names of three different animals, Store each animal name in a separate variable, Finally, print out the names of the animal in 3 lines
sessions.parentSummary: We began with how a program remembers things. Your child learned to create a variable — a labelled box that holds one piece of information — and to ask a question and store the answer. They can now write a short program that takes something you type and prints it back.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to explain a variable using something in the kitchen. A labelled jar is the analogy we used.
sessions.content: An introduction to what a programming language is and what Python is used for, then the three things every program needs: variables to hold information, data types to say what kind of information it is, and input to get it from the person using the program. Students print their first output with print().

sessions.title: The maths library
activities: Calculate the area of a circle
Take the length and breadth of a rectangle as decimals and print the area
Take a first and last name and print them swapped
sessions.task: First import math library at the beginning, Ask the user to enter the length of the side of a square. Calculate the area of the square using the formula: area = math.pow(side_length,2), Finally, Print out the calculated area
sessions.parentSummary: We introduced Python's built-in maths tools, and the difference between whole numbers, decimals and text — a distinction computers care about far more than people do. Your child wrote a program that asks for the side of a square and works out its area.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask what happens if you type a number as text by mistake. They have seen this break and can explain why.
sessions.content: Python's maths library, which supplies functions like powers and roots that are not built into the language itself. Alongside it, the difference between whole numbers, decimals and text — a distinction Python enforces strictly, and the source of most beginner errors.

sessions.title: Operators and averages
activities: Sum two variables using assignment operators
Take two numbers and report whether the sum is greater than, less than or equal to 5
Take three inputs and check whether all are equal, or any two are equal
sessions.task: Ask the user to enter the grades for five subjects. Arabic, English, Math, science and history. Calculate the total sum of the five subject, Use the total to calculate the average of the five grades. Finally, Print out the average
sessions.parentSummary: Arithmetic in code, and how a program compares two values to decide which is bigger. Your child built a small grade calculator: it takes marks for five subjects and returns the average.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Have them run their own report-card marks through it.
sessions.content: The two families of operator a program relies on: arithmetic ones that calculate, including floor division which discards the remainder, and comparison ones that ask whether two values are equal, greater or smaller. Comparisons are what later lets a program make decisions.

sessions.title: Making decisions
activities: Take the length and width of a rectangle and decide whether it is a square
Take a grade and decide whether the student passed
Take two numbers and print the greater
Apply a school grading scale from F through to A
sessions.task: Ask the user to enter a number, Check if the number is even or odd
sessions.parentSummary: The first big idea of the term: a program that chooses. Your child learned how code takes one path or another depending on what it finds. Their program decides whether a number is even or odd and says so.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to describe a morning routine as a set of “if… otherwise…” rules. That is exactly the structure they wrote.
sessions.content: Conditions, the first point at which a program chooses. An if condition tests a Boolean expression that is either true or false; when it is true the indented block runs, and when it is false the program skips it and carries on.

sessions.title: Shortcuts and flow
activities: Take three ages and determine the oldest
Decide whether a student may sit an exam based on attendance below 75%
Check whether a number is even
Apply a 5% bonus for employees with more than five years of service
sessions.task: Search about the word “Flow” in programming
sessions.parentSummary: More practice with decisions, plus the shorthand programmers use to update a stored value rather than rewriting it. This session's homework was reading rather than coding: a short piece of research on what “flow” means in a program.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask what they found out. Being able to explain it in their own words is the point.
sessions.content: More practice with conditions, plus the assignment operators that update a value in place — writing += rather than repeating the variable name. The session also introduces the idea of flow: the path execution takes through a program.

sessions.title: Repeating with for loops
activities: Print the even numbers from 0 to 100
Print the times table for any number the user enters
sessions.task: Ask the user to enter his name, Print it 5 times (using for loop)
sessions.parentSummary: Instead of writing the same instruction five times, your child learned to tell the computer to repeat it. This is the idea that makes programs short and powerful. They also met flowcharts — drawing a program as a diagram before writing any code.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to draw a flowchart for making a sandwich. Every step, in order, with a decision or two.
sessions.content: Loops, the structure that repeats steps under a condition. A for loop repeats a set number of times, and range() generates the sequence of numbers it walks through. It is explained through a box of toys: take one out, play with it, put it away, and keep going until the box is empty.

sessions.title: While loops and true/false
activities: Debug a broken program
Find every price in a shop below $10
Total the prices of all items below $10
sessions.task: To print first 10 integers and their squares, Using while loop
sessions.parentSummary: A second kind of repetition — one that keeps going until a condition stops being true — and the idea of a value that is only ever true or false. Their program printed the numbers 1 to 10 alongside each number squared.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask the difference between repeating something a set number of times and repeating it until something changes.
sessions.content: The second kind of loop: a while loop repeats as long as a condition stays true, rather than a fixed number of times. Introduced with Booleans — values that are only ever True or False — which is what the condition evaluates to.

sessions.title: Stopping and skipping
activities: Interview witnesses until the mystery is solved, using a loop of unknown length
Count to fifteen with a for loop, stopping at thirteen
sessions.task: Make a for loop to count first 15 numbers, Make it stop in number 13 and print it (using break)
sessions.parentSummary: A consolidation session. We revisited both kinds of loop and flowcharts, then added how to stop a loop early or skip a single step. A good week to check confidence — everything after this builds on loops.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask what “break” does. Stopping a search the moment you have found what you were looking for is the everyday version.
sessions.content: Controlling a loop from inside it. break stops the loop entirely; continue skips the rest of the current pass and moves to the next. The session also compares for and while loops and revisits pseudocode, planning a program in plain language before writing it.

sessions.title: Lists
activities: Track the practice scores of every player in a football team
Build a list of five student names, add a sixth and print it
sessions.task: Make a list and put on it a names of five students. Add a new student name to the same list and print it
sessions.parentSummary: Until now each variable held one thing. This session introduced lists — one name holding many items, like a shopping list. Your child also met pseudocode: writing out a plan in plain language before turning it into code.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to plan getting ready for school as numbered steps. That is pseudocode.
sessions.content: Lists: an ordered collection of values stored under one name, so a program can hold many things in a single variable. Items are reached by index, and the index operator can also reassign them.

sessions.title: Loops inside loops
activities: Draw a pattern of stars that grows on each line
Print a number pyramid using nested loops
sessions.task: Use nested loops to print a number pyramid pattern, The pattern should have multiple rows and columns, Each row should contain a sequence of numbers, Print out the pattern
sessions.parentSummary: One of the harder ideas in the level: putting a loop inside another loop, which is how programs produce grids and patterns. Your child printed a number pyramid — each row longer than the last.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to show you the pyramid and explain why each row grows. If they can, they have understood nesting.
sessions.content: Working through a list without knowing its length, using len() and a loop, and nesting one loop inside another to produce patterns. The session opens with a broken program the students have to diagnose.

sessions.title: Text and grids
activities: Change the sentence 'I love football' to 'I hate football'
Build a spelling practice program for a younger sibling
sessions.task: Create a research about 2-D Concepts
sessions.parentSummary: Working with text, and with data arranged in rows and columns — the structure behind a timetable, a spreadsheet or a chessboard. Homework was research rather than code this week.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask where they would find a grid of information in daily life. A bus timetable is a good one.
sessions.content: Strings treated as sequences of characters, so the same index operator that reaches into a list also reaches into text, including substrings. Then two-dimensional lists — a list of lists — walked with a nested for loop.

sessions.title: Functions — and the end of the level
activities: Write a program that calculates the area of a rectangle
Write a function that takes two numbers and prints their sum
sessions.task: Make a function to get two numbers from the user, And print the sum of them
sessions.parentSummary: The last building block of Level 1: functions. Your child learned to give a piece of code a name so it can be reused anywhere, instead of written out again each time. That completes the foundations — variables, decisions, loops, lists and functions. Level 2 puts them together into full projects and games.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to show you their favourite program from the term and talk you through it.
sessions.content: Functions: a named block of reusable code, explained through the structure of a song — a chorus written once and sung many times, rather than written out for every repeat. The last building block of the level.

sessions.title: Starting the noughts and crosses game
activities: Declare the game board and print it to the console
Ask the player which square they want to play in
Check the player's input is a legal move
sessions.task: Make a function to find positive numbers (using for loop). And use it to print positive numbers in this list ,my_numbers[-2,5,-10,8,-3,0,12]
sessions.parentSummary: Level 2 is built around four projects rather than exercises. Your child began a playable noughts and crosses game, pulling together the conditions, loops, lists and functions from Level 1 into one program.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them what a two-dimensional list is. A game board is exactly that: rows and columns.
sessions.content: Level 2 works through four full projects rather than exercises. The first is noughts and crosses, which needs everything from Level 1 at once: a two-dimensional list for the board, loops to print it, conditions to judge a move, and functions to organise the whole thing.

sessions.title: Randomness and where variables live
activities: Check for three in a row vertically
Check for three in a row diagonally
Write a function returning the largest of three numbers
sessions.task: Make a function to find the maximum of three numbers. Define the three variables as a local variable Write the steps To become successful through what you learned from today's hero
sessions.steamTopic: most successful athlete in the world
sessions.parentSummary: The game got an opponent that picks its own moves, using randomness. Your child also learned that a variable created inside a function cannot be seen outside it — a rule that causes confusion until it clicks.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Play a round against their program and see whether it puts up a fight.
sessions.content: Finishing the game with an opponent that chooses its own move using the random module, and the rules that decide a win. The session introduces variable scope — where in a program a variable can be seen — and software testing, running a program under different conditions to find where it fails.

sessions.title: A unit converter, part one
activities: Build the temperature conversion function
Write a function that sums all the numbers in a list
sessions.task: Make a function to sum all numbers in the list. The given list is:[8 , 2, 3 ,0 , 7] Create an research about Pharaohs
sessions.parentSummary: A new project: a program that converts between measuring units. This session was about the functions and arithmetic behind it.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to convert something for you and explain what the program does with the number.
sessions.content: A new project: a converter that changes measurements from one unit to another. This session covers the arithmetic behind it and the function structure that keeps each conversion separate and testable.

sessions.title: A unit converter, part two
activities: Build the length conversion function
Build the weight conversion function
Write the main function that routes between them
sessions.task: Write the steps to make anything fly
sessions.parentSummary: Finishing the converter, and a design-thinking exercise on how you would plan something complicated from scratch.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to talk you through how they broke the problem into pieces.
sessions.content: Completing the converter by adding length and weight conversions and a main function that ties them together, so one program offers several conversions behind a single menu.

sessions.title: An exam generator, part one
activities: Build the quiz creator's question store
Format the printed output so it reads as a paper
Remove the empty entries from a list of names
sessions.task: Make a program to To Remove empty strings from this list [“mike” , “  “ ,”Emily” , “Kelly” ,” “, “brad”] And print it after removing
sessions.parentSummary: A program that builds exam papers. Your child worked with text and grids of data, including cleaning up a list by removing the empty entries.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask why a program needs to check for blanks in data before using it.
sessions.content: The third project: a program that generates exam papers. It draws on strings, two-dimensional lists and functions, and introduces string formatting so the printed paper is laid out neatly rather than dumped to the console.

sessions.title: An exam generator, part two
activities: Ask which mode the user wants and check the teacher password
Add the teacher actions for creating questions
Average a list of numbers with a for loop
sessions.task: Make a list of numbers and add in it this numbers 10 ,20, 30,40,50, Get the average of this numbers and print it (using for loop)
sessions.parentSummary: Completing the exam generator with nested conditions and randomised question selection, so no two papers come out the same.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask it to generate you a paper and try to answer it.
sessions.content: Extending the exam generator with elif, which lets a program ask a second question when the first condition is false, and with user modes — a teacher who can add questions behind a password, and a student who can only sit the paper.

sessions.title: A restaurant ordering system, part one
keyConcepts: Project (First part of Restaurant ordering program)
activities: Build the menu and display it
Take an order from the customer
Write a function that checks whether a number is prime
sessions.task: Make a function that takes a number as a parameter, And check whether the number is prime or not
sessions.parentSummary: The final project: a program that takes food orders. Your child also wrote a function that checks whether a number is prime, which is a genuinely tricky piece of logic.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them how their program decides a number is prime. It has to rule out every possibility.
sessions.content: The final project: a restaurant ordering program. It works with strings and lists together, including join(), which turns a list into a single readable string — the difference between a raw list and a printed order.

sessions.title: Dictionaries, and finishing the order system
keyConcepts: Project (Second part of Restaurant ordering program)
activities: Add error handling to every function written so far
Calculate the total cost of an order
Research dictionary syntax
sessions.task: Make a research about the dictionary and how we use it (syntax)
sessions.parentSummary: The level closes with dictionaries, which store information in labelled pairs — a menu item and its price, for instance. That completed the ordering system and the level.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Order something from their restaurant program and check it adds up the bill correctly.
sessions.content: Dictionaries, which store data as key and value pairs rather than by position, so a menu item can be looked up by name. The session closes the level with error handling — catching bad input in a loop instead of letting the program crash.

sessions.title: First window with Tkinter
activities: Create a Tkinter window titled 'first project' and set its geometry
Add a text widget
Add a label widget
Place them with pack
sessions.task: Write a Python GUI program that imports Tkinter, creates a window and sets its title.
sessions.steamTopic: Strong numbers: when the factorials of the digits add up to the number itself
sessions.parentSummary: Level 3 leaves the black console window behind. Your child's Python programs now open a real window with text and labels in it, built with Tkinter — the library that comes with Python for exactly this.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to show you the window they made. Seeing their own program appear as a proper window is the moment this level turns on.
sessions.content: Graphical interfaces: the difference between a program that runs in the console and one with a window, buttons and text on screen. Tkinter is Python's standard library for building them. Everything in the window is a widget — a label for text you show, a text box for text the user types — and geometry decides the size of the window they sit in.

sessions.title: Events and reading the user's text
keyConcepts: Mouse, widget, keyboard and timer events
Reading text widget content with get()
activities: Build a program that prints whatever you type in the text widget into a label
sessions.task: Write a Python GUI program that creates a label, changes its font name, weight and size, and inserts the text 'hello'.
sessions.parentSummary: A window that does nothing is not much use, so this session was about events — code that runs when the user clicks, types or the clock ticks. Your child built a program that echoes whatever you type into a label.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask what an 'event' is in a program. Clicking, typing and even time passing all count.
sessions.content: Making the window respond. Tkinter events come in four kinds — mouse, widget, keyboard and timer — and a program can be told to run something when one happens. Alongside that, getting the content back out of a text widget so the program can use what was typed.

sessions.title: Arranging widgets: pack, grid and place
activities: Work through the layout exercises with different pack options
sessions.task: Write a Python GUI program that creates a Tkinter window with three labels arranged vertically using the pack geometry manager.
sessions.parentSummary: This session was about layout: the three different ways Tkinter can arrange things in a window, and which to use when. It is fiddly work, and it is what makes the difference between a window that looks thrown together and one that looks designed.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask why a program needs to be told where to put things. Nothing has a place until you give it one.
sessions.content: The three geometry managers and when each is right. Pack places widgets in position one after another, grid arranges them in a table of rows and columns, and place puts them at exact coordinates. Pack's options — padding, fill, expand, side and anchor — do most of the work at this stage. Radio buttons and extra windows are introduced alongside.

sessions.title: Buttons, entries and the click counter
keyConcepts: Styling widgets: font, width, height, background
activities: Build an app that counts clicks and shows the total in a label
Build an app that picks an image from a folder and displays it
sessions.task: Write a Python GUI program that adds a button using Tkinter, with the text 'quit', height 1 and width 35.
sessions.parentSummary: Buttons this week. Your child built a click counter — press the button and the number on screen goes up — which is the smallest program that has to remember something between clicks.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask what happens to the count when the program closes. Nothing is saved yet; that comes later.
sessions.content: The two widgets that make an application interactive: the Button, with its text, size, colours and the function it calls when pressed, and the Entry, a single-line box for user input. Checkboxes are covered too — a control with two states, on or off.

sessions.title: Message boxes, combo boxes and databases
activities: Build a form with labels and entry widgets for name, age, ID and email
sessions.task: Make a presentation about what you learned in the previous four sessions.
sessions.parentSummary: Your child's programs started talking back this week — pop-up messages, dropdown lists — and connected to a database, so a login page can check a real stored account rather than a name typed into the code.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Their task is a presentation on the first four sessions. Ask for it; explaining is where the gaps show up.
sessions.content: Widgets for choosing and warning: the message box that pops up to tell the user something, the combo box that drops down a list of options, and the popup menu. The session also connects the window to a MySQL database, which is what a login page needs to check a user against real stored accounts.

sessions.title: The text widget in depth
keyConcepts: Text widget properties: font, width, height, wrap
Inserting and deleting text from code
activities: Change the fonts and colours of a text widget and add a scrollbar
Insert, delete and re-insert text from code
Print the text content when a button is clicked, and clear it with another
sessions.task: Write a Python GUI program that implements a themed Entry widget with a different background and border colour.
sessions.parentSummary: A deeper session on the text box: how it wraps, how it scrolls, and how the program can change its appearance while it is running rather than only when it is created.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask what happens when you type more than fits. The answer — wrap or scroll — is a decision the programmer makes.
sessions.content: Everything the text widget can do: font, width in characters, height in lines, and how text wraps at the right edge. The config method changes any of these after the widget already exists, which is how a program restyles itself while running. Scrollbars are added for content that does not fit.

sessions.title: Frames and the grid layout
activities: Design a data entry form
sessions.task: Write a Python GUI program that designs a simple login form with labels and an entry widget, arranged with the grid geometry manager.
sessions.parentSummary: Your child designed a data entry form — the kind of screen you fill in online — using frames to group the fields and a grid to line them up. Getting a form to look tidy is harder than it sounds.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Look at any online form together and ask where the rows and columns are. They are always there, just invisible.
sessions.content: Building a real form. A frame is a rectangle used to group other widgets, both on screen and in the code, and a window can be split into several. The grid manager arranges widgets in rows and columns, which are configured first and can be made to span more than one cell.

sessions.title: Final project: the to-do list application
keyConcepts: Combining every widget from the level
Building a simple version before a complex one
activities: Build the simple version of the to-do list application
Extend it with a scrollbar, styling and button icons
sessions.task: Make a presentation about what you learned in the previous sessions.
sessions.parentSummary: The level ends with a real application: a to-do list your child can type into and add to. They built the plain version first and then made it look good — which is the right order, and not the order most people choose.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to show you the to-do list and add something to it. Then ask what they would add next.
sessions.content: The level closes with a complete application, built in two passes. The simple version makes a window with a title, a label, a text widget showing the tasks, an entry to type a new one and a button to add it. The complex version then adds a scrollbar, better fonts and colours, background styling and icons on the buttons.

sessions.title: Problem solving, conditions and functions
activities: Calculate the multiplication and sum of two numbers
Print the sum of the current number and the previous one
sessions.task: Write a program that asks the user for five numbers and then calculates and displays their average.
sessions.parentSummary: Level 4 is about solving problems rather than learning new syntax. This session set up the tools: expressions that come out true or false, conditions that act on them, and functions to package a solution once it works.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask what makes something an algorithm. A recipe is the usual answer, and it is a good one.
sessions.content: The level opens on problem solving as a method rather than a topic. Boolean expressions are what a program tests — an expression like 6 != 5 evaluates to true or false — and if-conditions act on the answer. Functions are revisited as the way a solved problem gets packaged for reuse, along with what happens when a program hits an error.

sessions.title: Logical operators and types of problem
activities: Work through problems that need more than one condition at once
sessions.task: Write a program that generates a random number between 1 and 10 and lets the user keep guessing, telling them each time whether their guess was too high or too low.
sessions.parentSummary: Your child learned to combine conditions — this and that, this or that — and looked at the difference between a problem with a yes/no answer and one where you are hunting for the best answer out of many.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Play the guessing game they wrote. Ask what strategy finds the number fastest; that is the next session.
sessions.content: Combining conditions with and, or and not, and a first look at how problems are classified: a decision problem asks whether something is true, while an optimisation problem asks for the best answer according to some score — the travelling salesman problem being the classic example.

sessions.title: Writing algorithms before writing code
keyConcepts: Advantages of writing the algorithm first
activities: Find the greatest of three numbers
Find the area of a rectangle
Swap two numbers using a third variable
sessions.task: Write down the steps you use to solve a programming problem.
sessions.parentSummary: This session was about planning before typing: writing the steps out in plain language first, then translating them into Python. Bugs are much easier to find in a plan than in code.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to write the steps for swapping what is in two cups using a third. That was the class exercise.
sessions.content: What makes a good algorithm: a definite procedure, step by step, easy to follow, easy to debug and independent of any programming language, so it can be turned into a real program afterwards. Worked through on small problems where the steps matter more than the syntax.

sessions.title: Handling errors and everyday calculations
activities: Check whether one number divides exactly into another
Calculate an average from a set of numbers
sessions.task: Python quiz.
sessions.parentSummary: What a program should do when something goes wrong was this week's topic — crash, or explain the problem and carry on. The class also covered remainders and averages, which turn up in almost every program.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask what their program does if you type a word where it wanted a number. Handling that gracefully is the skill.
sessions.content: Error handling — spotting problems, isolating them and keeping the program running rather than crashing, with useful messages instead of confusing ones. Applied to the everyday calculations that come up constantly in programs: averages, remainders and divisibility.

sessions.title: Loops and lists in depth
keyConcepts: The same algorithm in two languages
activities: Traverse a list of positions in reverse and act on each one
sessions.task: Write a program that checks whether a given word is a palindrome — that it reads the same forwards and backwards.
sessions.parentSummary: Loops and lists, at a level above where they started: going through a list backwards, and handling lists where each item is itself a bundle of information. The same problem was shown in two languages to make the point that the idea is the thing, not the syntax.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask what a palindrome is — that is their task this week — and whether they can name one.
sessions.content: For loops revisited and pushed further: iterating a list forwards and backwards, walking through a list of dictionaries, and using an index to reach each item. The same problem is shown in Python and JavaScript side by side, so the idea is clearly separate from the language.

sessions.title: Linear search and binary search
keyConcepts: Why binary search needs a sorted list
Comparing two strategies for the same problem
activities: Build the number guessing game and solve it with two different strategies
sessions.task: Write a program that counts the number of words in a given sentence.
sessions.parentSummary: Two ways to find something: checking every item one by one, or repeatedly halving the search. Your child implemented both on a number-guessing game and saw how much faster the second one is.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Guess a number between 1 and 100 and only say higher or lower. Seven guesses is enough if they halve each time.
sessions.content: Two ways to find something in a list. Linear search checks each item in turn from the beginning. Binary search jumps to the middle and throws away the half that cannot contain the answer, repeating until it is found — which is far faster, but only works if the list is sorted.

sessions.title: How fast an algorithm grows
keyConcepts: Comparing algorithms by growth, not by clock time
Finding the minimum and maximum in a list
