activities: Write a program that reads numbers until the user types 'done', then reports the smallest and the largest
sessions.task: Write a program that prints a number triangle using nested loops.
sessions.parentSummary: This session compared how two algorithms cope as the problem gets bigger — the question is not how long one run takes, but how much worse it gets when the list grows.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask which is faster for a list of a million items and why. The answer is not 'the faster computer'.
sessions.content: Comparing the two searches by how the work grows: linear search takes more steps at the same rate as the list gets longer, while binary search grows far more slowly. The same reasoning is applied to finding the smallest and largest number in a list.

sessions.title: Time complexity
keyConcepts: Reasoning about the cost of your own code
activities: Write a count_duplicates function and work out its time complexity
sessions.task: Python quiz.
sessions.parentSummary: Time complexity — the standard way programmers describe how an algorithm copes as the problem grows. Your child wrote a function and then had to work out how expensive it was, which is a genuinely advanced thing to ask.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask what O(n) means. 'Twice the data, twice the work' is the right idea.
sessions.content: Naming what the previous session measured. Linear search is O(n) and binary search is O(log n); other algorithms are polynomial or worse. The raffle example makes the categories concrete before the class writes a function and reasons about how expensive it is.

sessions.title: The limits of algorithms
keyConcepts: Problems that are too expensive to solve exactly
activities: Build a guess-the-animal game using a random search algorithm that tracks the number of guesses
sessions.task: Write the steps for making a professional program using the functions concept.
sessions.parentSummary: A session on what computers cannot do. Some problems have so many possible answers that checking them all would take longer than anyone has, and one famous problem cannot be solved by any program at all.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask how many routes there are between ten houses. The answer — over three million — usually lands well.
sessions.content: Where algorithms run out. The travelling salesman problem can be solved by checking every route, but the number of routes grows by factorial — ten houses is already over three million paths — so checking them all stops being practical very quickly. The halting problem is introduced as something no algorithm can decide at all.

sessions.title: Recursion
keyConcepts: Reducing a problem to a smaller one
activities: Write a recursive function that sums the numbers from 0 to 10
Find the largest number in a list recursively
sessions.parentSummary: The course finishes with recursion — a function that calls itself, solving a big problem by solving a slightly smaller version of it over and over. It is the idea most people find hardest and most satisfying.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Two mirrors facing each other is the usual way in. Ask them to explain recursion using it.
sessions.content: A function that calls itself. Recursion solves a problem by reducing it to a smaller version of the same problem, until the smallest case can be answered directly — adding the numbers from 1 to 7 becomes 7 plus the answer for 1 to 6, and so on down.

sessions.title: Introduction to Motors & Coding
keyConcepts: What is a motor? (Electrical → Mechanical energy)
How motors work in simple machines
activities: Build a motorcycle model
Program: Adjust speed to 9 and time to 10 sec
Experiment with different speed settings
sessions.task: Research the frog life cycle
sessions.steamTopic: Motors and what they are used for
sessions.parentSummary: The first build. Your child learned what a motor actually does — turning electricity into movement — then built a motorcycle and programmed how fast and how long it runs.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them what a motor turns electricity into. Movement is the answer, and they built one.
sessions.content: The first build, and the first idea: a motor turns electrical energy into movement. The session looks at where motors appear in everyday machines, then puts one in a motorcycle model and controls it from blocks — speed, direction and how long it runs.

sessions.title: Sensors & Life Cycles
activities: Build a frog model with moving parts
Program: Continuous forward/backward motion (5 sec intervals)
Add sound effects to frog movement
sessions.task: Research lion habits and behaviors
sessions.steamTopic: The life cycle of a frog
sessions.parentSummary: A frog model that hops backwards and forwards on a loop, with sound. Your child used repetition in a program for the first time, and researched the frog life cycle alongside it.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to tell you the stages of a frog's life. It was their homework and it fits the model they built.
sessions.content: A frog model, matched to its science topic: the frog life cycle, and the repeated hop that gives the program its first loop. Sound blocks are added so the model makes a noise as it moves.

sessions.title: Display & Advanced Coding
activities: Build a lion model
Program: Display name/age with custom background
Adjust speed to 7 for 2 sec movements
sessions.task: Compare lion habits to other big cats
sessions.steamTopic: The life cycle of a lion
sessions.parentSummary: A lion model, plus getting the program to display text and use a custom background. Your child also stored information like a name and age for the program to use.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to make their program say your name.
sessions.content: Getting the program to show something on screen as well as move a model. Text and a custom background are displayed, and information such as a name and an age is stored for the program to use — a first variable, without the word.

sessions.title: Magnetism
activities: Build swing attraction model
Program: Set speed to 7, time to 2 sec with added sound
Test different sound effects
sessions.task: Research common uses of sensors
sessions.parentSummary: Magnetism — which materials are attracted and which are not, and how a speaker uses magnets to make sound. Your child built a swinging fairground model.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Go round the kitchen with a magnet and ask them to predict what will stick.
sessions.content: Magnetism: which materials are attracted and which are not, and how a speaker uses a magnet to turn an electrical signal into sound. The swing attraction model is built and programmed with movement and a sound effect.

sessions.title: Human Senses vs. Robot Sensors
activities: Build shark model
Program sensor-triggered movements
Compare human and robot sensing abilities
sessions.task: Research gear mechanisms
sessions.steamTopic: Sensors, and whether humans are like robots
sessions.parentSummary: Comparing human senses with robot sensors. Your child built a shark that reacts to what it detects, and discussed where a robot's senses fall short of ours.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask which human sense is hardest for a robot to copy.
sessions.content: Sensors, opened with a question the class argues about — are humans like robots? A sensor is how a machine notices anything at all, and the shark model reacts to what its sensor detects rather than running a fixed sequence.

sessions.title: Gears & Motion
keyConcepts: How to change speed using Gears
activities: Build spinner model
Experiment with different gear setups
Use different gear configurations
sessions.task: Research motion sensor applications
sessions.parentSummary: Gears — how teeth interlock, how gears reverse direction and how they trade speed for power. Your child built a spinner and tested different gear arrangements.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them why a bicycle has gears. They can now explain it properly.
sessions.content: Gears and the three things they are used for: changing speed, changing direction, and carrying movement from one place to another. The spinner build shows the speed change directly — swap the gears and the same motor spins it differently.

sessions.title: Motion Sensor & Energy
activities: Build racing car model
Program motion-activated movements
Test different sensor modes
sessions.task: Research sources of energy
sessions.parentSummary: A racing car that starts when it detects movement, plus energy: where it comes from, and the difference between sources that run out and those that do not.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to name a renewable energy source and one that is not.
sessions.content: Energy and the forms it takes, then the motion sensor, which detects something moving nearby. The racing car build uses it, so the car reacts to what passes rather than only to the program.

sessions.title: Tilt Sensor & Renewable Energy
activities: Build Milo science rover
Program tilt-controlled movements
Final project presentations
Final Task: Comprehensive presentation on gears and sensors
sessions.steamTopic: Renewable and non-renewable sources of energy
sessions.parentSummary: The level ends with the Milo rover, controlled by tilting, and a presentation on everything learned about gears and sensors. Presenting their own work is part of the assessment.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask for the presentation. Explaining it out loud is where the learning settles.
sessions.content: Where energy comes from — renewable sources against non-renewable ones, and which is better and why. The tilt sensor is introduced, which reports how the model is being held, and the hungry crocodile game uses it.

sessions.title: Lunar Rover & Space Exploration
activities: Build lunar rover model
Program rover movements
sessions.task: Research first person on moon
sessions.steamTopic: Space exploration and the moon landing
sessions.parentSummary: Level 2 opens with space. Your child built a lunar rover and programmed it to cross difficult ground, then researched the first person to walk on the moon.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them who first walked on the moon, and what makes driving on it so hard.
sessions.content: Level 2 opens with space. A lunar rover has to cross ground nobody has prepared for it, which is a build problem before it is a programming one, and the class researches the first person to walk on the moon alongside it.

sessions.title: Forklift & Gear Systems
keyConcepts: How can i control speed using gears
activities: Build forklift model
Test lifting capacity
Adjust gear configurations
sessions.task: Draw/label gear types
sessions.parentSummary: A working forklift. Your child tested how much it could lift and changed the gears to find out how that affects lifting power.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them what changing the gears did to the lifting. Slower but stronger is the trade.
sessions.content: Gears again, now for lifting rather than spinning. The forklift build asks how much it can raise, and changing the gearing changes the answer — the trade between speed and force made concrete.

sessions.title: Windmill & Renewable Energy
activities: Build windmill model
Test blade angles
sessions.task: Research another renewable source
sessions.parentSummary: A windmill, and how moving air becomes electricity. Your child tested different blade angles to find which generated most power.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask which blade angle worked best. They tested it rather than guessing.
sessions.content: Renewable energy, and a windmill that turns moving air into electricity. Students test different blade angles to find which generates most, which makes it an experiment rather than a demonstration.

sessions.title: Smartbin & Recycling Tech
activities: Build smart bin model
Play recycling game
Program sensor triggers
sessions.task: Create paper bin prototype
sessions.parentSummary: A smart bin that opens when it detects someone approaching, plus how recycling sorting actually works.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them what happens to a plastic bottle after it goes in the recycling.
sessions.content: Recycling — how waste is sorted and why it matters — followed by the motion sensor. The smart bin opens when it detects someone coming, which is a machine reacting to the world without being told to.

sessions.title: Carousel & Gearbox Mechanics
activities: Build carousel model
Test rotation speeds
Adjust gearbox setup
sessions.task: Research monkey species
sessions.parentSummary: A carousel driven by a gearbox, and how rotation is passed from one part of a machine to another. Your child tuned the gearbox to change the speed.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to run it fast and slow, and explain what they changed.
sessions.content: The gearbox: several gears working together so one motor can drive something at a chosen speed. The carousel is built on one, and tuning the gearbox changes how fast it turns.

sessions.title: Monkey & Biomechanics
activities: Build monkey model
Simulate climbing motions
Program swinging actions
sessions.task: Research sports benefits
sessions.parentSummary: A monkey model that climbs and swings, comparing how animals move with how robots do. Copying a living thing's motion is harder than it looks.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask what a real monkey can do that their model cannot.
sessions.content: Copying an animal. The monkey model climbs and swings, which is a harder mechanical problem than rolling on wheels, and the session compares how a living thing moves with how a robot does.

sessions.title: Sports Robot & Athletic Tech
activities: Build sports robot
Program athletic motions
sessions.task: Research drawing bots
sessions.parentSummary: A sports robot, and a look at how robotics is used in real athletics — training aids, timing and analysis.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them how a robot could help someone get better at a sport.
sessions.content: Robotics in sport — the training aids, timing systems and analysis behind modern athletics — and a sports robot built and programmed to perform a movement of its own.

sessions.title: Drawing Bot & Robotic Art
activities: Build drawing bot
Program geometric shapes
sessions.task: (None - celebration session)
sessions.parentSummary: The final build: a robot that draws. Your child programmed movement along two axes to produce geometric shapes, which is drawing by pure instruction. The session doubles as a celebration of the whole course.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask it to draw you something, and keep it.
sessions.content: The final build is a drawing robot: movement along two axes, combined in the right order, produces a shape. Drawing by pure instruction, with nothing left to the hand. The session doubles as the course celebration.

sessions.title: Introduction to Coding, EDP, and HTML Basics
keyConcepts: Difference between a website and a web server (e.g., Chrome as a browser vs hosting servers)
Introduction to frontend development languages: HTML, CSS, JavaScript
activities: Create the basic structure of a portfolio website
Write a meaningful title and a short introduction using appropriate text tags
sessions.task: Define a problem: pick a problem in your community and research it.
sessions.steamTopic: What is code and what is computer code?
sessions.parentSummary: What a website actually is, the difference between what runs in your browser and what runs on a server, and the first HTML. Your child started the portfolio site they will build across the whole level.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them the difference between a browser and a website. Most adults get this wrong.
sessions.content: What a website is and where it runs — the browser on your machine against the server it came from — and the split between frontend and backend. Then the first HTML: the doctype that declares the version, the head that holds information for machines, the body that holds what people see, and the text tags. The Engineering Design Process starts here too, one step per session, beginning with defining the problem.

sessions.title: HTML Elements, Attributes, and Layout Building
keyConcepts: HTML attributes and how they modify elements
a tag (links) and its attributes (href, target, etc.)
image tag and its attributes (src, alt, width, etc.)
button tag and its attributes (onclick, type, etc.)
ul, ol, li (List tags and their attributes)
table, tr, td, th (Table tags and structure)
activities: Add a navigation menu using a list
Add images and icons to the portfolio
Add an experience section using paragraphs, lists, or a table
sessions.task: Keep researching the problem you chose, and work out why it is a problem.
sessions.parentSummary: Links, images and buttons, and how attributes change what an element does. Your child added a navigation menu and an experience section to their portfolio.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to show you their site so far and click through the menu.
sessions.content: Attributes, which change what an element does: href on a link, src and alt on an image, type and onclick on a button. Lists and tables give the page structure, and the same tags make a navigation menu and an experience section.

sessions.title: Multimedia & User Input Elements
keyConcepts: video tag and its attributes (controls, src, poster, etc.)
audio tag and its attributes (controls, autoplay, etc.)
Introduction to input types (text, email, checkbox, etc.)
form tag and common attributes (action, method, etc.)
activities: Add a button to view/download the CV
Create a contact section using a form
Add navigational arrow buttons using images or icons
sessions.task: Research the problem further — understand its causes and its consequences.
sessions.steamTopic: What is sound and how is it represented digitally
sessions.parentSummary: Video, audio, embedded maps and forms. Your child added a contact form and a CV download button to the portfolio.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Fill in their contact form and ask what happens to what you typed.
sessions.content: Everything on a page that is not text: video, audio, and iframes for embedding a map or a video from elsewhere. Then forms — the input types for text, email, numbers, dates, checkboxes and radio buttons, and the attributes that name each field so the submitted data can be read.

sessions.title: CSS Basics & Structure Styling
keyConcepts: <div> and <span> tags for layout and inline grouping
activities: Add class and ID attributes to structure elements in the portfolio
Create an external CSS file and link it to the project
Begin styling selected components using CSS
sessions.task: Start collecting what you need for your project, and save it on your computer.
sessions.parentSummary: CSS — the language that controls how a page looks, kept separate from the HTML that says what is on it. Your child set up a stylesheet and began styling the portfolio.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask why the appearance is kept in a different file from the content.
sessions.content: CSS, which controls how a page looks while HTML says what is on it. A rule picks an element with a selector and sets its properties. Class selectors, written with a dot, apply to many elements; id selectors, written with a hash, apply to one. Div and span group things so they can be styled together.

sessions.title: Advanced Selectors & Layout Styling
keyConcepts: CSS border, margin, and padding properties
activities: Apply a general style to the portfolio
Style the profile, about, experience, and contact sections individually using margins, paddings, and colors
sessions.task: Research solutions that would meet the requirements of your project.
sessions.steamTopic: Understanding the technology behind Microsoft Word and formatting logic
sessions.parentSummary: Choosing precisely which parts of a page to style, plus colours, backgrounds, spacing and hover effects. The portfolio starts looking designed rather than assembled.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Hover over things on their site and see what reacts.
sessions.content: Making things look designed rather than default: border width, style, colour and radius; backgrounds, including how an image repeats or does not; and the spacing that separates one part of a page from another.

sessions.title: Dimensions, Typography & Positioning
keyConcepts: CSS properties for height and width
CSS display property: block, inline, inline-block, none
CSS position property: static, relative, absolute, fixed, sticky
activities: Update all text elements with appropriate font and text styles
Apply different display options to structure layout
Add positioning to relevant sections (e.g., fixed navigation bar or sticky contact button)
sessions.task: Start building a prototype — apply what you have learned to your own website.
sessions.steamTopic: Introduction to the Cartesian coordinate system
sessions.parentSummary: Typography and positioning — fonts, sizes, alignment, and how elements sit relative to one another. Layout is where most beginners struggle, so this session matters.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to explain why one section sits beside another instead of below it.
sessions.content: Type and layout. Colour, horizontal and vertical alignment, and text direction control how words sit on the page; list styling controls the markers; and the display property decides whether an element takes a whole line or sits beside its neighbours.

sessions.title: UI/UX Concepts & Visual Styling
keyConcepts: CSS transitions (smooth changes for hover effects, buttons, etc.)
activities: Style and enhance the navigation bar (hover effects, spacing, colors)
Apply transitions and transforms to key elements (like buttons or image effects)
sessions.task: Continue building your prototype.
sessions.steamTopic: Introduction to UI/UX Design principles (how users interact with interfaces)
sessions.parentSummary: Interface design, and animation: smooth transitions, scaling and rotation. Your child polished the navigation bar and added movement to buttons.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them what makes a website feel good to use rather than just look good.
sessions.content: Tables styled properly — collapsed borders, rounded corners, alignment within cells — and transitions, which make a change happen over time instead of instantly. Applied to the navigation bar, which is where most users notice it. The STEM slot covers UI and UX design: how a thing looks against how it feels to use.

sessions.title: Open Source & Portfolio Finalization
keyConcepts: Create the complete website that students have been working on across previous sessions, applying all steps of the EDP process
Integrate all learned components: HTML structure, media elements, forms, CSS styling, layout techniques, and UI/UX considerations
Ensure the final site is structured, styled, and functional
sessions.task: Share your website with your friends — upload it to GitHub or to Google Drive.
sessions.parentSummary: The portfolio is finished and pulled together — every technique from the first seven sessions in one site. Your child also learned what open source means.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask for the full tour. This is the first substantial thing they have built.
sessions.content: The last step of the Engineering Design Process: share your findings. Students finish the EDP project they have been building since session one and put it somewhere other people can see it. The STEM slot looks at open source and how it changed what software is.

sessions.title: Introduction to JavaScript & Variables
activities: Create the HTML structure for a Quiz website
sessions.task: Research the difference between scripting and procedural programming languages.
sessions.parentSummary: JavaScript begins — the language that makes a page do things rather than just display them. Your child started building a quiz site.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them what the three web languages are for. Structure, appearance, behaviour.
sessions.content: JavaScript, which makes a page do things rather than just show them. Variables are declared with var, let or const, with rules about what a name may contain, and the arithmetic operators work as expected. The quiz project that runs to the end of the level starts here.

sessions.title: JavaScript Functions & Logic
keyConcepts: Conditions in JavaScript (if, else, else if)
Combining functions with conditions to add logic
activities: Add logic and interactivity to the Quiz Website
Use conditions to check answers and give feedback
Style the website using CSS
sessions.task: Prepare a presentation about scripting programming languages.
sessions.steamTopic: What is a function in programming
sessions.parentSummary: Conditions and functions in JavaScript, used to make the quiz check answers and respond.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Take their quiz and get one wrong deliberately to see what it says.
sessions.content: Functions in JavaScript — a named block that runs when called — and conditions with if and else. The two combine to give the quiz project its logic, while the CSS from earlier sessions gives it its appearance.

sessions.title: DOM Manipulation & Events
keyConcepts: Introduction to the DOM (Document Object Model)
Accessing DOM elements using JavaScript (getElementById, querySelector, etc.)
activities: Build an Interactive Color-Changing Game where clicking elements changes their colors dynamically
sessions.task: Pick a problem in your community and research it.
sessions.parentSummary: How JavaScript reaches into a page and changes it while it is running, and how it responds to clicks. Your child built a colour-changing game.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Play it and ask how the page changes without reloading.
sessions.content: The DOM: the page as a structure a program can reach into. Changing innerHTML replaces content, setting a style property restyles an element, and setAttribute changes an attribute — which is how a page responds to a click instead of reloading.

sessions.title: Digital Citizenship & Problem Solving with JS
keyConcepts: Apply JavaScript problem-solving to real use cases
Debugging and testing basic JS logic
sessions.task: Pick a problem in your community and research it.
sessions.parentSummary: The level closes with debugging practice and a discussion of online safety and behaving well on the internet — a fitting end for people who can now build web pages themselves.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask what responsibilities come with being able to build a website.
sessions.content: Putting loops, arrays and conditions together on a real calculation — averaging a set of scores and then judging the result — and a closing look at staying safe online.

sessions.title: Review & Project Kickoff
keyConcepts: HTML Revision: Lists, Tables, Forms, Labels, Headings, Paragraphs, Links, Images, and Divisions
CSS Revision: Colors, Fonts, Text Alignment
JavaScript Revision: Data types, Variables, Functions, console.log()
activities: Build a recap project (choose one)
Hobbies Website
Animals Website
Sports Website
Use HTML, CSS, and JS to apply all reviewed content
sessions.task: Study the flashcards made in the session, and add more questions and answers to them.
sessions.parentSummary: Level 2 opens with a recap project of your child's choosing, rebuilding everything from Level 1 in one site before moving on to harder material.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask which theme they chose and why.
sessions.content: A deliberate revision session, opening with why revision works at all. Everything from Level 1 is pulled back: the HTML document structure, CSS, and the DOM as the interface that lets a program change a page. Students then pick a topic — animals, sports or a hobby — for the project they build across the level.

sessions.title: Semantic Structure & Wireframing
keyConcepts: HTML Semantic Elements: header, article, nav, main, section, aside, footer, figure
activities: Restructure an old project using semantic HTML
sessions.task: Look at Facebook's login page and draw a wireframe of it.
sessions.steamTopic: Introduction to Wireframes: What they are and why they matter
sessions.parentSummary: Writing HTML that describes what each part of a page means, not just how it looks. This is what lets screen readers and search engines make sense of a site. Your child also met wireframing.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask how a blind person uses a website. Semantic HTML is a large part of the answer.
sessions.content: Planning a page before building it, the way a house gets a blueprint first. Semantic structure means choosing tags for what the content is rather than how it looks, and the session makes the case for the alt attribute on every image — for the people who cannot see it, and for when the image fails to load.

sessions.title: Responsive Design & Media Queries
keyConcepts: Using Fluid Grids and Flexible Layouts
Writing and applying Media Queries to handle different screen sizes
activities: Begin the Facebook Login Page Clone – Part 1
Create the HTML structure
Apply semantic layout
Begin styling with responsiveness in mind
sessions.task: Research responsiveness principles and tools not covered in the session, to discuss next time.
sessions.parentSummary: Making a site work on any screen size. Your child started a Facebook login page clone, building it to adapt from phone to desktop.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Open their page and resize the window. It should rearrange itself.
sessions.content: Making one page work on every screen. Media queries apply different styles at different widths, using the and, not and only keywords to say exactly when. The STEM slot covers aspect ratios — why there are black bars at the edges of some video.

sessions.title: Layout Hierarchy & Grid Systems
keyConcepts: CSS Grid: Rows, columns, and gap properties
Basic Flexbox Concepts: justify-content, align-items, and flexible layouts
Continued practice with Media Queries for responsiveness
activities: Complete Facebook Login Page Clone – Part 2
sessions.task: Prepare a presentation on which responsive design principle you find most effective.
sessions.parentSummary: Proper layout tools — grids and flexible boxes — which replace the awkward workarounds beginners rely on. The login clone was finished with them.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to compare their new layout with how they would have done it in Level 1.
sessions.content: CSS Grid, which lays a page out in rows and columns defined up front, with named areas, automatic sizing and gaps. The STEM slot covers visual hierarchy: how a design decides the order in which you read it, usually without you noticing.

sessions.title: Animations & Visual Enhancement
activities: Build an Art Gallery Website
sessions.task: Research animation tools such as Canva and how they differ, to discuss next time.
sessions.parentSummary: Animation: keyframes, transitions and hover effects, applied to an art gallery site. Restraint matters here as much as capability.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them when an animation helps and when it just annoys.
sessions.content: CSS animation. Keyframes describe what changes and when, and animation-fill-mode decides what the element looks like before it starts and after it ends. Applied to a page with a header, a hero section and a gallery.

sessions.title: Abstraction & Bootstrap Basics
keyConcepts: When to use predefined vs. custom styles
Bootstrap Grid System for responsive layout
activities: Create a Travel Blog Website
sessions.task: Prepare a presentation about frontend frameworks for other programming languages.
sessions.steamTopic: Abstraction in Computing: Focusing on essentials and hiding unnecessary complexity
sessions.parentSummary: Bootstrap, a ready-made set of components, and the judgement of when to use someone else's work versus writing your own. Your child built a travel blog with it.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them what they gained by using Bootstrap, and what they gave up.
sessions.content: Abstraction — ignoring the detail that does not matter for the job in hand — and Bootstrap as an example of it: a framework of ready-made components and styles, against writing every rule yourself. One is faster, the other gives complete control.

sessions.title: Creative Coding & Modern JavaScript
keyConcepts: Arrow Functions in JavaScript: Concise function syntax
Destructuring in JavaScript for cleaner variable assignments
activities: Create a Quiz Game
sessions.task: Research why electrical wires are connected in series or in parallel, and what each is for.
sessions.parentSummary: Modern JavaScript syntax — shorter ways of writing the same logic, and clearer rules about which values can change. Your child built a quiz game.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them to show you the old way and the new way of writing the same function.
sessions.content: The three places JavaScript can run: in the browser console with F12, on your own machine through Node.js, or in an online editor. Students then build a quiz with cards, styling and logic of their own.

sessions.title: Asynchronous Programming & Flow
activities: Build a Magic Website
sessions.task: Prepare a presentation on how we protect our pages from cyber criminals.
sessions.parentSummary: Code that waits. Your child learned the difference between instructions that run in order and ones that carry on while something else finishes — the idea behind a page that stays responsive while loading.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask why a website can stay usable while it is still loading something.
sessions.content: Why JavaScript does not freeze while it waits. The event loop is explained as a person working a to-do list: the call stack is what is being done now, web APIs are the helpers working in the background, and finished work joins a queue to be picked up — with urgent work jumping ahead.

sessions.title: Web Security Basics
keyConcepts: How to Prevent XSS in HTML & JavaScript
activities: Enhance the Facebook Clone Project
Add validation and security-friendly code
Improve layout and ensure clean user interaction
sessions.task: Play the security game from the session, to discuss next time.
sessions.steamTopic: Introduction to Cookies and Cybersecurity Concepts
sessions.parentSummary: Web security: the three goals every secure system aims at, how attacks get in through unchecked input, and why you never trust what a user types. Your child hardened the login clone.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them why a website should never trust what you type into it.
sessions.content: Web security. Confidentiality, integrity and availability as the three things being protected, and cross-site scripting as the worked example: an attacker leaves a script in a comment, and it runs in the browser of everyone who reads it. The defence is to never trust user input without cleaning it first.

sessions.title: SEO and Interactive Design
activities: Create an Interactive Product Showcase Website
sessions.task: Research version control systems, to discuss next time.
sessions.parentSummary: How search engines find and rank a site, and what a developer can do about it. Your child built an interactive product showcase.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them what makes one page appear above another in search results.
sessions.content: Search engine optimisation — how a page ends up on the first results page rather than the tenth. The title tag and meta description are what a search engine shows, and heading tags give the content a hierarchy that both search engines and readers use.

sessions.title: Git, GitHub, and Web Collaboration
keyConcepts: What is Git? and why version control matters
What is a version in code?
Installing GitHub and setting it up
Key concepts: Repository, Branch, and Commit
activities: Create a Recipe Finder Website
sessions.task: Build a small web project, push it to GitHub with Git, and bring the repository link next time.
sessions.parentSummary: Version control with Git and GitHub — how professionals track changes and work together without overwriting each other. Your child started a recipe finder site.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask them what a commit is. Saving with a note explaining what changed is close enough.
sessions.content: Version control. A commit is a snapshot with a note saying what changed, and a branch is a separate line of work that can be merged back — so an experiment does not put the working version at risk. The STEM slot covers IP addresses and DNS.

sessions.title: Deployment and Web Publishing
keyConcepts: Steps to Deploy a Website using GitHub Pages
activities: Complete and Deploy the Recipe Finder Website
Finalize design, test responsiveness, and publish it online
sessions.steamTopic: What is the Difference Between HTTP and HTTPS?
sessions.parentSummary: The course ends with deployment: your child published a website to the internet with a real address anyone can visit.
sessions.parentHomeActivity: Ask for the link. Their site is genuinely live, and that deserves a look.
sessions.content: Publishing. GitHub Pages hosts a site straight from a repository at no cost and with no server to manage, so pushing a change updates the live site. The course ends with each student's project actually online. The STEM slot covers the difference between HTTP and HTTPS.
